frus-1969-76ve09p1-d21.summary: This is a long study prepared on July 6, 1973 by a State Department-led interagency group for the White House (under NSSM 185) on U.S. policy toward Libya. It reviews the Qadhafi regime, U.S. interests (oil, about 2,800 American citizens in Libya, Libya's strategic position) and options ranging from improving relations to confrontation. It notes that relations were at a low point after Libyan fighters fired on an American reconnaissance plane near Tripoli and an American oil company was nationalized.
tripoli_details: Libya declared a 'restricted area' within a 100-mile radius of Tripoli International Airport and claimed the right to control aircraft and ships entering it.
On 21 March 1973 Libyan fighter aircraft fired at an unarmed USAF C-130 reconnaissance plane flying inside that zone.

The study says diplomats and couriers accredited in Tripoli were denied entry because their passports lacked an Arabic translation, and American Embassy personnel could not leave since replacements could not be sent.
It expected that a Libyan-Egyptian union would reduce embassies in Tripoli to a lower status.
It records that Libyans demonstrated in June 1967 and February 1973 but otherwise showed little political activism.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d134.summary: On July 30, 1980 the State Department's Executive Secretary, Peter Tarnoff, sent Brzezinski a history of U.S.-Libyan relations from the 1969 revolution to 1980. It says relations stayed troubled, with brief hopes of improvement in 1975 and 1979, and explains the U.S. decisions to keep only a chargé d'affaires in Tripoli and to block sales of military aircraft such as C-130s.
tripoli_details: After Wheelus Air Force Base was forced to close in June 1970, the Embassy found it nearly impossible to get appointments with anyone but middle-level Foreign Ministry officials.
In early 1973 the U.S. decided to keep an official presence in Tripoli headed by a chargé d'affaires rather than an ambassador.
In April 1975 Libya said it had lifted the ceiling on U.S. Embassy personnel in Tripoli.
Under Secretary Newsom met Major Jallud in Tripoli in June 1979 for frank but promising talks.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d74.summary: This is National Intelligence Estimate 36.5-71 of April 30, 1971, assessing Libyan policy under the Revolutionary Command Council (RCC). Analysts judged the 28-year-old Colonel Qadhafi's regime was secure enough to last, that it had won popular credit by evicting Western bases and raising oil income, and that it was turning to Egypt, France and the Soviet bloc for military help.
tripoli_details: The estimate says the Tripolitanean Police and the Cyrenaican Defense Force were disbanded because they might have been focal points for discontent.
It reports that expelling the resident Italian community (15,000-20,000 people) in mid-1970 removed most skilled artisans and modern-sector farmers in Tripolitania.
It says a handful of Egyptians were at Ukbah Bin Nafi (formerly Wheelus) Air Base, used by the Libyan Air Force.
It says Cairo received about $160 million from Tripoli in the last year.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d53.summary: In Telegram 10936 of August 14, 1976, the U.S. Embassy in Cairo told Kissinger that Egypt's President Sadat had decided Qadhafi was a dangerous 'lunatic' who must be removed. The embassy described Egyptian troops massing on the Libyan border and weighed Egypt's options, from engineering a coup to a limited or full military attack.
tripoli_details: The embassy said assassination squads targeting Egyptian notables were first sent from Tripoli in summer 1975.
It reported that Egyptian forces in the western desert (over 10,000 troops) could, with reinforcements, mount an attack as far as Tripoli under favorable conditions.
One option it listed was a brigade-size airborne raid on Tripoli to destroy Qadhafi and his government.
It said Egypt was still sending a new ambassador to Tripoli despite Qadhafi's threat to sever relations on September 1.
It cited an August 8 bomb attack in central Cairo as the latest Libyan terrorist action.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d100.summary: This June 1, 1979 CIA intelligence memorandum, 'Libya's Changing Role as a Patron State,' judges that Qadhafi remained a major patron of terrorists but had changed tactics since late 1977 to improve his image in the West. It reports reduced help to Irish and European groups and some cooperation with Western governments.
tripoli_details: Libya invited the head of the State Department's Office for Combatting Terrorism to visit Tripoli, and the visit took place in January 1979.
The memo says an Italian claimed to have seen underwater training of Red Brigades members at a facility outside Tripoli.
It says 'Carlos' was housed at 'The Institute,' a terrorist training camp near Tripoli.
It counts 12 terrorist training camps in Libya in 1979, at least four used by Palestinian groups, compared with 20 in 1970.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d54.summary: This September 1, 1976 State Department intelligence report, 'Qadhafi: The Increased Threat,' argues that Qadhafi had moved beyond isolated terrorist acts and could now destabilize the Middle East and Africa, citing his $7 billion yearly oil revenue. It lists Libyan-backed plots against Sudan's Numayri, Egypt, Tunisia and others, and Libyan support for Uganda's Idi Amin.
tripoli_details: A senior Egyptian diplomat in Tripoli said Qadhafi was determined to topple Sudan's Numayri.
Libyan officials arrested two Egyptian security men on August 24 aboard a chartered Egypt Air flight from Cairo to Tripoli, which Egypt called 'an act of air piracy.'
The report says Tripoli sent radar equipment to Uganda and may have sent troops.
Libyan commando teams were caught in operations to kidnap or assassinate Libyan opponents abroad, including the nominal Foreign Minister in Rome.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d32.summary: This August 19, 1974 CIA intelligence memorandum examines the growing feud between Libya's Qadhafi and Egypt's Sadat. It says Sadat had recalled Egypt's ambassador and withdrawn Egypt's military mission from Libya, that Qadhafi was increasingly isolated, and that the Soviets were improving ties with Libya through a major arms deal.
tripoli_details: Sadat recalled Egypt's ambassador and withdrew the entire Egyptian military mission in Libya.
The memo says the Libyan people were happy to see the Egyptians go, though many educated Libyans understood Libya's dependence on Egyptian goodwill.
Jallud visited Moscow in May 1974 and Libya concluded a major arms deal with the Soviet Union.
Sadat offered to send an emissary to Tripoli for reconciliation talks.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d131.summary: This May 16, 1980 CIA intelligence memorandum judges that Libya might be entering a more dangerous phase of support for terrorism. It points to the November 1979 burning of the U.S. embassy in Tripoli, Qadhafi's feud with moderate Palestinians, and his willingness to target heads of state.
tripoli_details: The April 1980 summit of the Steadfastness and Confrontation Front was held in Tripoli.
The memo calls the sacking of the U.S. embassy in Tripoli in November 1979 a crude imitation of the seizure of the U.S. embassy in Tehran.
It also mentions the burning of the French embassy in Tripoli.
Libyans reportedly trained dissidents from Tanzania, Rwanda, Mozambique, South Africa and Namibia at a camp south of Tripoli.
Qadhafi hindered a Cuban effort to move Ugandan cadets to Havana via Tripoli.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d77.summary: This May 17, 1971 memorandum is a CIA status report on Libya covering the period from early 1971. It describes the effect of Nasser's death, Soviet tanks arriving in Tripoli, the successful oil-company settlements, and at least seven counter-coup attempts in the first sixteen months after the revolution.
tripoli_details: Soviet tanks and other military hardware arrived in Tripoli on 18 July 1970.
Negotiations with Western oil companies opened in Tripoli in late February 1971 and were completed on 2 April, giving a five-year agreement.
The report says at least seven counter-coup attempts occurred within Libya in the first sixteen months after the revolution, plus one launched from Chad.
CIA was monitoring two further counter-coup plans, one led by former Libyan military officers abroad.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d101.summary: This is the record of a June 17, 1979 meeting in Tripoli between Under Secretary of State David Newsom and Major Abd al-Salam Jallud, described as number two to Colonel Qadhafi. Newsom explained the U.S. interest in better relations, while Jallud said Libya would not change its position on the Palestinian issue to improve bilateral ties.
tripoli_details: The meeting took place in Tripoli on June 17, 1979 as part of the Newsom mission.
Jallud said the mission followed a Palestinian meeting held in Tripoli.
Marshall Tito had recently visited Tripoli and passed Qadhafi's comments about lack of contact with the U.S.
Madfai was the Libyan chargé d'affaires who responded quickly to the U.S. proposal.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d45.summary: These are minutes of a November 24, 1969 Washington Special Actions Group meeting on Libya, shortly after the coup. Officials discussed contingency plans, including a military-supported evacuation of Americans, and the coming talks on the future of Wheelus Air Base starting December 15.
tripoli_details: Newsom said the planned evacuation of U.S. citizens would have U.S. forces enter through Wheelus.
The Libyans would not permit resumption of training activities at Wheelus and wanted the U.S. to withdraw, so the best the U.S. could expect was about one more year there.
Unarmed aircraft were still operating in and out of Wheelus, but the U.S. Phantoms stationed there were embarrassing to the Libyan government.
Talks with the Libyans on Wheelus were to begin December 15.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d25.summary: On September 17, 1973 Assistant Secretary Newsom sent Kissinger a follow-on options paper on U.S. policy toward Libya (NSSM 185). It weighs continuing present policy, sending a special emissary, or harsher steps, and warns that tougher options could lead Libya to close the U.S. Embassy in Tripoli.
tripoli_details: One option was to keep a small mission going in Tripoli without accrediting a new ambassador.
The paper warned that some options could result in Libyan closure of the American Embassy in Tripoli and nationalization of remaining U.S. oil assets.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d44.summary: On November 20, 1969 NSC staff members Behr and Saunders sent Kissinger a summary and critique of a paper on possible pressures against Libya's new regime. It covers the Wheelus base question, the regime's insecurity, and U.S. oil investment valued at $5 billion, and weighs options such as delaying a reply on Wheelus or cutting oil purchases.
tripoli_details: The Libyans asked the U.S. to leave Wheelus before December 24, 1971; the U.S. planned to agree in principle to early withdrawal and propose detailed discussions.
The paper said a delay on Wheelus could lead the regime to open a street campaign endangering the U.S. community, base and Embassy.
It noted that the former King had moved to Egypt that month and the Crown Prince was in jail, and that other possible contenders were under surveillance in Benghazi.
It said 90 percent of Libya's 3 million barrels a day was produced by twenty-eight American companies.
A landing of forces at Wheelus was listed as an option to consider for evacuating Americans.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d50.summary: This December 30, 1969 National Intelligence Estimate, 'Short-Term Prospects for Libya,' assesses the new Revolutionary Command Council shortly after the September coup. Analysts judged the council wanted to remove the Western bases at Wheelus, Tobruk and El Adem, had no clear program beyond that, and had not sought close ties with the USSR.
tripoli_details: The estimate says the 6,000 US and British military personnel in the country at the time of the revolution were seen as a potential threat to Libya, whose armed forces numbered only about 8,000.
It judged the Libyans intended to use Wheelus as a military airfield and might hire civilian contractors or ask Egypt for technicians to run it.
It reported that a Soviet offer of military assistance made right after the revolution was rejected.
Soviet diplomats complained of difficulty reaching RCC members and of harassment by low-ranking Libyan military personnel.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d106.summary: In this October 4, 1979 cable, Secretary of State Vance reported his 45-minute talk in New York with Libyan Foreign Minister Turayki. Vance said the U.S. did not want to undermine the Libyan government but objected to Libyan support for terrorism, and he proposed exchanging high-level visits and cultural exchanges.
tripoli_details: Vance hoped a senior official such as Saunders or Newsom could visit Tripoli soon.
Turayki praised U.S. Chargé Eagleton for strengthening relations in Tripoli and suggested a committee based in Tripoli to review bilateral relations.

frus-1981-88v24-d66.summary: In this January 30, 1986 cable the U.S. Embassy in Algiers reported on a meeting between Algerian leaders and Qadhafi in a remote desert location, at which Qadhafi asked Algeria to pass a message to the United States. The embassy said Algeria saw the meeting as a success because it controlled the media and gained concessions on Tunisia and the Western Sahara.
tripoli_details: The embassy said the remote desert location let the Algerians prevent any pro-Qadhafi demonstrations.
It said Algeria obtained concessions from Qadhafi on Tunisia, support for Ben Bella and the Western Sahara.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d94.summary: In Telegram 1699 of October 30, 1972, the departing U.S. Ambassador to Libya, Joseph Palmer, reported a farewell meeting of an hour and a half with Qadhafi at his office in the Aliziya barracks. Qadhafi complained the U.S. had not delivered on contracts and armed Israel, while Prime Minister Jallud said the Palestine cause was a matter of life and death.
tripoli_details: The meeting took place on the evening of October 28, 1972 in Qadhafi's office at the Aliziya barracks.
Present were Prime Minister Jallud, Foreign Minister Kikhya, Chief of Staff Abu Bayr Yunis and RCC member Hamza.
Qadhafi said the evacuation of Wheelus had been resolved more easily than expected.
The day before, Qadhafi spoke at an intellectuals' seminar in Tripoli about steering clear of major powers.

frus-1981-88v24-d10.summary: In this August 10, 1981 cable, the U.S. Embassy in Algiers reported that Algeria's Foreign Ministry asked for U.S. views on rising tension between Libya and Egypt/Sudan. Algeria planned to send a high-level delegation to Tripoli to urge moderation on Qadhafi and feared a superpower confrontation.
tripoli_details: The Algerians planned to send a very high-level delegation to Tripoli in a week or ten days to press Libya to be more conciliatory.
The embassy judged Algeria feared a U.S. move against Qadhafi directly or through Egypt and Sudan.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d22.summary: These are minutes of an August 14, 1973 Senior Review Group meeting on U.S. policy toward Libya, chaired by Kissinger. Participants debated whether to send an emissary, punish Libya or buy it off, and discussed a cable from the U.S. mission in Tripoli arguing against approving new military equipment for Libya.
tripoli_details: Kissinger referred to Tripoli telegram 1044 of August 13, in which the chargé argued against approving new military equipment for Libya without getting something besides money.
Sisco suggested loosening relations with Libya and coordinating with oil companies to apply leverage on Qadhafi.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d104.summary: On August 7, 1979 CIA's National Foreign Assessment Center director Bowie sent Brzezinski a note assessing nationalized American oil assets in Libya and compensation. The CIA expected disputes between Tripoli and the companies over valuation and judged Libya could replace U.S. technical services with European firms.
tripoli_details: The note says Libya could probably get good terms by giving non-U.S. firms access to crude denied to the nationalized U.S. companies.
It expected valuation disputes between Tripoli and the companies.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d44.summary: On July 7, 1975 NSC staffer Robert Oakley sent Scowcroft a memo, 'The Libyan Threat,' drawing on a CIA study of the Soviet-Libyan arms relationship. It reported a major expansion of Soviet arms deals including jets, bombers, submarines and tanks, and Soviet port-call rights.
tripoli_details: Kosygin recently visited Tripoli.
Tripoli apparently agreed to allow Soviet ships occasional port calls for bunkering and replenishment under tight Libyan controls.
The Libyans may be dangling greater concessions such as base rights to get Soviet help in building naval facilities at Tobruk.

frus-1981-88v24-d159.summary: This April 20, 1986 cable from the U.S. Embassy in Algiers reports Algerian reaction to the U.S. strikes on Libya. An Algerian official said Algeria had sent a party official to Tripoli to warn Qadhafi about terrorism just before the strikes and that Qadhafi had denied involvement.
tripoli_details: Party Permanent Secretary Messaadia was sent to Tripoli to warn Qadhafi on terrorism just before the U.S. strikes, according to Belkheir.
Belkheir said news of the strikes had mobilized Algerian public opinion on Qadhafi's side and that he banned TV coverage of foreign demonstrations.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d63.summary: This July 31, 1970 CIA intelligence memorandum reviews where Libya got its weapons after the 1969 revolution. It says Britain had been the main supplier, that U.S. military aid ran from 1957 to 1970, and that the Soviet Union suddenly delivered tanks and artillery on 18 July 1970.
tripoli_details: Wheelus Air Base was handed over to the Libyans on 11 June 1970, after which the U.S. military aid group was reduced to a five-man liaison section attached to the U.S. Embassy.
The Soviet Union made an overt delivery of tanks and artillery on 18 July 1970.
A special envoy from the Soviet Defense Ministry visited Tripoli as early as 19 September 1969.
The memo says U.S. military aid to Libya from 1957 to 1970 totaled about $33 million, and Libya's fleet included nine F-5s and three C-130s among 30 aircraft.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d71.summary: In Telegram 373 of February 24, 1971, the U.S. Ambassador in Tripoli reported a 1 hour 45 minute meeting with Qadhafi at the Aziziyah barracks. Qadhafi said the only real issue between the two countries was the Arab-Israeli dispute, but he still wanted the F-5 aircraft the U.S. had not delivered.
tripoli_details: The meeting was held February 23, 1971 at the Aziziyah barracks, with Foreign Minister Kikhya and Marthinsen the only others present.
Qadhafi arrived in casual sport attire and was relaxed and cordial.
Qadhafi said young officers had been optimistic when the U.S. Air Force evacuated Wheelus that good relations would follow.
The telegram was repeated to the consulate in Benghazi.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d90.summary: On July 28, 1972 Deputy Secretary of State Irwin sent Secretary Rogers an action memorandum on Libya. Irwin said he favored delivering the F-5 aircraft the U.S. had contracted to sell, without demanding anything specific on the oil company dispute, to remove an irritant and open the way to less hostile talks.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d94.summary: In this September 21, 1978 cable the State Department told the U.S. Embassy in Tripoli to be cautious about reports of Qadhafi's interest in better relations. It said the U.S. would keep refusing senior-level talks, but would consult Congress on selling two Boeing 727s with guarantees they be used only commercially.
tripoli_details: The Department said it was pleased the embassy was setting up a channel to Qadhafi.
It warned the Libyans that ad hominem attacks on President Carter or injury to U.S. persons or property would be resented by Congress.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d125.summary: On February 1, 1980 Secretary of State Vance sent President Carter a memo on the future of the U.S. Embassy in Tripoli. He recommended keeping the mission at its minimum size of eight or fewer, offering only minimal consular services until after the exchange of Egyptian and Israeli ambassadors, because of the risk of another attack like the one on December 2.
tripoli_details: The U.S. chargé returned to Tripoli December 31, 1979 expecting to be received by Qadhafi, but there had been no response to Carter's January 17 message.
The memo says the weight of intelligence evidence suggested Qadhafi himself authorized the December 2 attack on the Embassy to prove his government was as 'revolutionary' as the Iranians.
Vance recommended the mission stay at eight people or fewer and reexamine its status in mid-March.
An Afro-Arab meeting planned in Tripoli that month was postponed because Libya insisted on excluding Egypt.
Vance proposed delivering the President's message to the Foreign Minister if Qadhafi would not receive Chargé Eagleton.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d96.summary: On December 13, 1972 the State Department's Deputy Assistant Secretary Ross wrote about the Libyan Ambassador's alleged involvement in terrorism after an FBI report. Attached is an Embassy Tripoli airgram saying the Tripoli newspaper al-Fajr al-Jadid reflected the government's unease about terrorism outside Israel and the Arab states.
tripoli_details: The Tripoli daily al-Fajr al-Jadid on November 14, 1972 ran a report on 'Secret Decisions of the American Government against Arabs Residing in the United States,' which the embassy called an authoritative mouthpiece for the regime.
Qadhafi gave an October 7 speech in Tripoli praising the Japanese perpetrators of the Lod Airport massacre.
Libya granted asylum to commandos freed by the Lufthansa hijackers.

frus-1981-88v24-d252.summary: In this January 9, 1986 cable the U.S. Ambassador in Rabat reported an audience with Morocco's King Hassan on dealing with Libya after President Reagan's January 7 announcement on terrorism. Hassan said Qadhafi was deeply frightened and had phoned him, and said he was sending Royal Counselor Guedira to Tripoli.
tripoli_details: Hassan said he was sending Royal Counselor Reda Guedira to Tripoli on January 9 to see what Qadhafi would do.
The ambassador told Hassan the U.S. wanted a halt to Libyan behavior, including expulsion of Abu Nidal.
He noted that Qadhafi first praised the December 27 terrorist attacks in Rome and Vienna and only later condemned them.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d53.summary: This February 13, 1970 CIA intelligence memorandum is an assessment of Libya's new military regime. It says the junta was still insecure, noted that the ministers of defense and interior were arrested in December 1969, and reported that 1,500 to 2,000 Egyptian soldiers were stationed in Benghazi and Tripoli.
tripoli_details: Some 1,500 to 2,000 Egyptian soldiers were stationed in Benghazi and Tripoli, beginning in December 1969, with about 500 more in military, security and communications posts.
In December 1969 the ministers of defense and interior were arrested before they could make a planned move against their colleagues.
The memo said the Egyptian units could keep control of an air- or beach-head if foreign moves were made to topple the regime.
It noted the quick U.S. decision to meet Libyan demands to evacuate Wheelus Air Base.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d43.summary: In Telegram 711 of June 18, 1975, the U.S. Embassy in Tripoli sent its annual policy assessment for Libya. It judged that the main danger of a Soviet military presence in Libya was that it strengthened Qadhafi's hand against a peaceful Arab-Israeli settlement, and that the regime's basic anti-communist orientation had not changed.
tripoli_details: The embassy believed the regime's basic anti-communist orientation would not change as long as Qadhafi was in power.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d124.summary: In this January 19, 1980 cable the U.S. chargé, Eagleton, reported that he called on Ahmad Shahati, head of Libya's Foreign Liaison Office, asking to be received by Qadhafi to deliver a message from President Carter. Shahati was noncommittal, though he asked whether this was the time to get 'the aircraft' passed through Congress.
tripoli_details: Eagleton said he could go to Benghazi to see Qadhafi at any time, and that Ali al Houdairi was due in Tripoli January 26.
Shahati joked or half-joked that Qadhafi would receive the American representative if the Americans in Tripoli set up a 'People's Bureau.'
Eagleton read the Afghanistan portion of Carter's message to Shahati, and said Qadhafi was to be interviewed by Harry Reasoner of CBS in Benghazi a week later.
Eagleton said he was reachable for a few days through the U.S. Embassy in Tunis.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d203.summary: This June 19, 1979 cable from the U.S. Embassy in Rome reports Under Secretary Newsom's June 18 meeting in Tunis with Tunisian Prime Minister Nouira after Newsom's visit to Tripoli. Nouira described cool Tunisian-Libyan relations, supported the U.S. ban on aircraft exports to Libya, and doubted Qadhafi would moderate.
tripoli_details: Newsom had been asked to visit Tripoli to discuss relations following Libyan messages, most recently conveyed through Marshal Tito.
Nouira supported the U.S. export ban on aircraft for Libya.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d96.summary: This October 21, 1978 State Department cable reports Acting Secretary Newsom's meeting with Libyan Foreign Secretary Turayki. They discussed Chad, southern Africa and Libya's image in Congress as a supporter of terrorism, and the meeting ended cordially with Turayki suggesting a visit to Tripoli.
tripoli_details: Newsom said a recent Arab-American Dialogue held in Tripoli had served a useful function.
Turayki suggested that Newsom or the Secretary visit Tripoli.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d143.summary: In this December 9, 1980 cable the State Department told posts about its reply to a Libyan protest over U.S. military maneuvers in Egypt. Washington said the exercises were not hostile to Libya and urged both Egypt and Libya to show restraint along their border, while noting the note's tone did not match earlier hints of improved relations.
tripoli_details: The Department said that when the U.S. representative returned from Tripoli he had indicated the Jamahiriya wanted improved relations, which the tone of the protest note did not bear out.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d93.summary: This October 17, 1972 cable reports Secretary Rogers' meeting with Libyan Foreign Minister Kikhia. Kikhia said the main problem was the U.S. failure to deliver contracted F-5 aircraft, while Rogers said the U.S. was concerned about apparent Libyan interference in other states and about terrorism.
tripoli_details: Kikhia said Libya's Mirage inventory was supposed to reach 100 but then stood at about 30.

Kikhia said that after the Wheelus agreement Libya concluded there should be no remaining complications with the U.S., and that more than 80 percent of petroleum activity in Libya was by U.S. companies.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d29.summary: On November 23, 1973 Assistant Secretary Newsom sent Kissinger a briefing memo on possible pressure points against Libya. He concluded the U.S. had little leverage, listing options from breaking relations to freezing assets, denying export licenses and banning oil-industry equipment, and warning most could provoke nationalization of remaining U.S. oil holdings.
tripoli_details: The memo said about 2,000 Americans lived in Libya, mostly oil company employees and dependents.
It said Libya had been without a Foreign Minister for nearly a year and its Embassy in Washington had been headed by a junior first secretary for more than six months.
It reported about seven hundred Libyan students in the United States.
It judged there was no identifiable focus of dissidence in Libya around which a political action program could be built.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d3.summary: In this February 18, 1977 cable the U.S. Embassy in Tunis reported a Tunisian-Libyan dispute over an Italian drilling ship working off the coast on the continental shelf. Libya's Prime Minister Jallud reportedly warned that Libyan forces would 'open fire' if Tunisia did not stop 'occupying' the rig.
tripoli_details: On Jan 18 the Libyan Foreign Ministry sent a circular note to all diplomatic missions in Tripoli except Tunisia's about the drilling operation, and a second note on Feb 1 with corrected coordinates.
On February 17 Jallud called in the Tunisian High Representative in Tripoli and threatened that Libyan forces would 'open fire.'
The drilling ship was the Scarabeo Four, owned by an AGIP/SAIPEM subsidiary of Italy's ENI.

frus-1981-88v24-d319.summary: This November 17, 1984 State Department cable reports Secretary Shultz's November 14 meeting with Tunisian Defense Minister Baly. Baly stressed the Libyan threat to Tunisia, including the Moroccan-Libyan accord and Libyan troops withdrawn from Chad now on the Tunisian border, and Shultz said the U.S. shared the view of Qadhafi and aimed to isolate him.
tripoli_details: Baly said Qadhafi believed the May 8 attack (on Qadhafi's compound) was fomented by Tunisia, the U.S. and the UK, and that participants crossed into Libya from Tunisia.
Baly said Qadhafi accused Tunisia of boycotting the OAU meeting in Tripoli to keep him from the OAU presidency.
Baly said Libyan troops withdrawn from Chad were on Tunisia's border shouting anti-Tunisian slogans.
Shultz called Qadhafi 'a terrorist and an aggressor.'

frus-1981-88v24-d63.summary: In this December 18, 1985 cable the U.S. Embassy in Tunis reported Tunisian Foreign Minister Caid Essebsi's views on Algerian-Libyan contacts and Tunisian-Libyan relations. He said Tunisia would not resume diplomatic relations with Tripoli unless Libya compensated Tunisia for losses from its expulsions of Tunisian workers.
tripoli_details: Essebsi said there was no hope of Tunis resuming relations with Tripoli without compensation for Libya's expulsion of Tunisian workers.
He reported that Libya had sent a high-level delegation to Algerian President Bendjedid urging him to meet Qadhafi.
He said Algeria would not receive Qadhafi in Algiers but at an unspecified location.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d2.summary: In this January 20, 1977 cable the U.S. Embassy in Tripoli reported on the Egyptian Ambassador's views of Egyptian-Libyan relations, which he called bad and deteriorating. The ambassador said Egypt would step up pressure on Qadhafi, felt insecure in Tripoli, and suggested the U.S. 'should get rid of him.'
tripoli_details: The Egyptian Ambassador said he felt somewhat insecure in Tripoli and that his embassy might face open attack if Egyptian or Sudanese military intervention occurred.
He said Egyptian radio now reached every home in Tripoli and that exiled RCC member Muhayshi would be used on it.
He said Libyan sabotage in Egypt and frozen Egyptian accounts in Libyan banks of about 17 million were Egyptian complaints.
Marshal Tito was in Tripoli at the time.
Egypt had had vague approaches from Prime Minister Jallud and thought RCC member Kharoubi might lead an eastern Libya.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d84.summary: This February 28, 1977 CIA intelligence memorandum describes Qadhafi's plan to reshape the Libyan government into a 'people's democracy.' Analysts judged he faced weakened support in the military since a 1975 coup attempt and aimed to sideline the Revolutionary Command Council.
tripoli_details: The memo says a 1975 coup attempt engineered by council member Umar Muhayshi and army officers exposed wide dissatisfaction with Qadhafi's one-man rule.
It reports at least several attempts on Qadhafi's life since 1975, and that he replaced suspected officers with kinsmen and members of tribes from his home region.
It says Qadhafi orchestrated numerous popular demonstrations to show his support.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d4.summary: In this March 29, 1977 cable the U.S. Embassy in Tunis reported Tunisian Prime Minister Nouira's account of the continental shelf confrontation with Libya. Nouira said Tunisia wanted the dispute sent to the International Court of Justice and that Foreign Minister Chatty had spent two hours with Qadhafi, who refused to negotiate away a meter of territory.
tripoli_details: Foreign Minister Chatty visited Tripoli the week before carrying a note for Qadhafi.
Qadhafi told Chatty he would not negotiate away a single meter of Libyan territory.

frus-1981-88v24-d405.summary: This January 3, 1983 State Department cable explains U.S. policy on the Organization of African Unity's crisis. It says Qadhafi's bid to chair the OAU failed when two summit attempts in Tripoli lacked a quorum, and that the U.S. did not lobby to prevent a quorum.
tripoli_details: An OAU summit in Tripoli in August 1982 failed for lack of a quorum, and a second attempt known as 'Tripoli II' in November also failed.
A pre-summit ministerial meeting was called for November 15 in Tripoli for a November 23-26 summit.
The Department said the U.S. did not lobby anyone to prevent a quorum at Tripoli.

frus-1981-88v24-d160.summary: This May 1, 1986 cable reports Under Secretary Armacost's April 28 talks in Washington with Algerian official Hamdani about Libya and the Western Sahara, soon after the U.S. air strikes. Armacost said the U.S. aimed to isolate Qadhafi and objected to Algeria's dialogue with him, while Hamdani said the U.S. policy of isolation had not worked.
tripoli_details: Hamdani said Qadhafi was disliked in Algeria before the U.S. bombings but voices in the FLN supported him afterward.
Armacost said Qadhafi had isolated himself by attacks on Chad and Tunisia.

frus-1981-88v24-d168.summary: This July 11, 1987 State Department cable relays the Algerian Ambassador's readout on Algerian-Libyan contacts after a Qadhafi visit to Algiers. The ambassador said Algeria was responding to Libyan initiatives cautiously, and Bendjedid wanted involvement in Libya so as to 'neutralize' Qadhafi.
tripoli_details: Sahnoun said Libyan military officers had come to Algiers to appeal for support in lessening Libya's isolation.
A document on future Algerian-Libyan relations was drawn up during a Jalloud visit about a week before Qadhafi's visit.

frus-1981-88v24-d23.summary: In this July 19, 1983 cable the U.S. Embassy in Tunis reported that Tunisian Prime Minister Mzali was leaving for Tripoli to attend a session of the Tunisian-Libyan High Commission. The embassy said Tunisia still saw Qadhafi's Libya as a security threat and the main issues were Tunisian workers enrolled in Libyan-backed 'liberation movements' and the continental shelf.
tripoli_details: Mzali traveled to Tripoli on July 19, 1983 for the High Commission session; Tunisian ministers of Economy and Plans had been there since July 17.
The embassy said the Libyans would have taken great offense if Mzali had not gone.
The High Commission had been dormant until revived by Qadhafi's visit to Tunisia in February 1982.

frus-1981-88v24-d34.summary: In this May 14, 1984 cable the U.S. Embassy in Tunis reported escalating Libyan threats against Tunisia after infiltrators entered Libya. Libyan statements blamed 'a Tunisian side' for the infiltration, and Libya admitted holding three Tunisian personnel.
tripoli_details: A statement said to represent Libyan 'masses' who demonstrated in Tripoli on May 13 accused Egypt, Sudan and elements in the Tunisian regime of conspiring with 'stray dogs.'
The Libyans admitted in a May 10 statement that they were holding three Tunisian personnel.
The embassy thought a negotiated solution was still possible if Tunisia gave Qadhafi an official expression of regret and private assurances.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d13.summary: These April 16, 1973 minutes of a Washington Special Actions Group meeting covered Libya and Indochina. Kissinger said the U.S. Chargé in Tripoli had sent many messages, and that the rules of engagement for U.S. reconnaissance flights over the Mediterranean needed to be carefully drawn since Libyans were willing to shoot at planes fifty miles out at sea.
tripoli_details: Kissinger said the chargé in Tripoli had sent more messages in a week than the Ambassador in Cambodia sent in a year.
He said Libyans were willing to shoot down American planes at a range of fifty miles out at sea.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d117.summary: This memorandum records a December 19, 1979 meeting in Washington between Under Secretary Newsom and Ali El-Houderi of the Libyan People's Bureau after the attack on the U.S. Embassy in Tripoli. El-Houderi said Libya regretted the attack, would pay compensation and promised protection for Americans, while Newsom raised the detention of embassy fiscal officer Bashir Dultz.
tripoli_details: El-Houderi said Libya accepted responsibility for failing to protect the Embassy and was prepared to pay compensation for the damage.
Newsom asked that security units be designated to protect the Embassy and that Chargé Eagleton get an early meeting with Qadhafi.
Bashir Dultz, a German national who had been the Embassy's budget and fiscal officer for many years, was arrested and detained, which caused nervousness among Embassy employees.
El-Houderi said Dultz was well known in Tripoli and many believed he was a 'spy.'

frus-1977-80v17p3-d88.summary: In this April 14, 1977 cable the U.S. Embassy in Tripoli reported the Libyan response to a message from President Carter. A Libyan official said Libya wanted better political relations, and a Libyan note denied that the terrorist known as Carlos had entered Libya except once when he transited Tripoli airport.
tripoli_details: The Libyan note said Carlos entered Libya only on the occasion of the Oil Minister's kidnapping, when he transited Tripoli International Airport.
The note said Libya wanted Carlos for trial for killing a member of the Libyan delegation at the OPEC conference in Vienna.
The Libyan official said only he and Turayki in the Tripoli Foreign Office knew of the President's letter.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d95.summary: This October 2, 1978 cable reports Under Secretary Newsom's one-hour meeting at the UN with Libyan Permanent Representative Kikhia. Newsom said he would see if relations could improve, but military items like C-130s were blocked because of Libyan support for terrorism, while Kikhia said the U.S. needed a scapegoat.
tripoli_details: Kikhia said about 4,000 U.S. citizens worked in Libya and 3,000 Libyan students were in the U.S.
He said the U.S. imported about 40 percent of Libyan oil at an annual cost of 4 billion dollars.
A US-Arab Dialogue was scheduled for Tripoli later that week.
Newsom noted agreement had been given to export 400 Oshkosh trucks.

frus-1981-88v24-d56.summary: This July 1985 State Department cable instructs the U.S. Embassy in Rabat to press Morocco on its union with Libya. It voices concern at reports that King Hassan might visit Qadhafi in Tripoli, at a new joint 'defense affairs committee,' and at Libyan accords with Iran and Sudan.
tripoli_details: The Department asked whether Morocco's Basri traveled to Tripoli to challenge Qadhafi on his Iranian ties or to arrange a visit by the King.
It said it hoped Hassan would never make the trip to Tripoli.
It reported unconfirmed claims that Qadhafi had renewed financial support to the Polisario.
It cited concern over a reported military agreement between Libya and Sudan.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d82.summary: On February 14, 1977 Secretary of State Vance sent President Carter a memo on U.S. relations with Libya and Iraq. On Libya, he said relations had deteriorated since Qadhafi's 1969 takeover, with embassies headed by chargés since November 1972, and listed Libya's ejection of the U.S. from Wheelus, an attack on a C-130, oil nationalizations and the 1973 oil embargo.
tripoli_details: Between 1969 and 1974 the Libyans ejected the U.S. from Wheelus Air Base, attacked an unarmed American C-130, nationalized U.S. oil interests and expelled American missionaries.
Nearly 10 percent of U.S. crude imports came from Libya, representing about 30 percent of Libya's production.
Approximately 2,000 Americans lived in Libya and about 2,000 Libyans studied at U.S. institutions.
The U.S. had denied export licenses for eight C-130 aircraft Libya bought in 1972 from Lockheed.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d69.summary: This December 31, 1970 briefing memo to Secretary Rogers concerns whether to deliver F-5 aircraft contracted by the pre-revolution Libyan government. The African Affairs bureau, like Ambassador Palmer, favored delivery, while the Near East bureau warned of congressional criticism and pressure from Israel's supporters.
tripoli_details: The memo noted that despite the U.S. withdrawal from Wheelus, attempts to maintain good relations had been basically one-sided.
It mentioned the contract's 'changed circumstances' clause that might justify non-delivery.

frus-1981-88v24-d54.summary: This May 20, 1985 memo from Assistant Secretaries Murphy and Crocker to Secretary Shultz reports King Hassan's May 16 comments on Libya. Hassan called Qadhafi an 'unbalanced child' and secretly said he, Qadhafi and Chad's Habre would sign an agreement bringing Chad into the Moroccan-Libyan 'Arab-African Union.'
tripoli_details: Hassan said he probably would have to visit Tripoli 'some day, but not right away.'
U.S. official Teicher cited the dangerous 'Voice of Vengeance' broadcasts, Libyan subversion in Tunisia and Libyan provision of Scud rockets to Iran.
Murphy said Qadhafi had never foresworn terrorist activity, and Foreign Minister Filali said Qadhafi sought international acceptance.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d39.summary: This September 16, 1969 intelligence memorandum offers initial thoughts on the Libyan coup of the same month. It says US and UK forces were in Libya when the coup occurred, notes the new government had said nothing yet about Wheelus, and expects an aggressive anti-Israeli posture that would cause problems for the U.S.
tripoli_details: At the time of the coup there were some 1,100 British troops near Tobruk and Wheelus held some 5,000 American personnel.
The memo noted the new government had made no move against Wheelus and the British facilities, and judged it probably would eventually.
It suggested the Revolutionary Command Council's conciliatory statements might be dissimulation to reduce the threat of counterrevolutionary intervention.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d51.summary: In this April 24, 1976 cable, Assistant Secretary Atherton praised the U.S. Chargé in Libya, Carle, for his report of talks with Qadhafi after a long desert trip. He instructed Carle to remind Libya of obstacles to accepting a Libyan ambassador, including hostile Libyan statements and support for terrorists.
tripoli_details: The Department congratulated the chargé on an 'arduous desert excursion' to meet Qadhafi (reported in Tripoli telegrams 546 and 548).
It cited Libya's cable to 72 heads of state, remarks at the FAO meeting in Rome in November 1975 and an Al Jihad article of March 5 as examples of unwelcome attacks on the U.S.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d132.summary: This May 30, 1980 National Intelligence Daily article, 'Libya: Eliminating the Opposition,' says Qadhafi's purges at home and killings of dissidents abroad had deepened discontent to dangerous levels. CIA analysts reported perhaps 2,000 arrests since February, scattered riots, perhaps four assassination attempts and nine murders by hit squads abroad.
tripoli_details: Perhaps 2,000 people were arrested beginning in February 1980, first bureaucrats then senior military officers and members of the 'people's committees.'
The article reported scattered local riots and perhaps four assassination attempts against Qadhafi, the latest the week before.
Qadhafi reportedly wore a bullet-proof vest and lived in a mobile 'command van.'
Hit squad murders abroad totaled nine: two in London, four in Rome, one in Beirut, one in Bonn and one in Athens on 21 May.
A Libyan student was kidnapped in London by members of the Libyan 'people's bureau.'
Death was prescribed in April 1979 as the punishment for economic crimes.

frus-1981-88v24-d85.summary: This January 16, 1988 State Department intelligence cable, 'Belling the Libyan Cat,' says Algeria, Tunisia and Mauritania were willing to admit Qadhafi to their regional pact if he met their price. It notes Libya agreed to pay ousted Tunisian workers and stop sheltering Tunisian dissidents in return for renewed diplomatic ties.
tripoli_details: Algerian President Bendjedid visited Tunis and Tripoli to remove remaining obstacles.
Qadhafi was set to visit Tunis but cancelled when Tunis received the Sixth Fleet Commander on January 11-13.
King Hassan ended his 'union' with Qadhafi in 1986 under U.S. pressure, but the cable said Rabat and Tripoli retained intelligence links.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d26.summary: In this September 1973 cable the State Department told the Embassy in Tripoli it must find a way around Libya's rule requiring Arabic translation in passports. It proposed a bilingual rubber stamp for U.S. officials traveling to Libya, so staff, especially communicators and secretaries, could be replaced.
tripoli_details: The Department said every other major country represented in Libya had agreed to put Arabic in its passports in some form.
It proposed as a test case to seek a visa for a communicator to replace Schauer.
It noted that even the Swiss had used an Arabic stamp to preserve their Embassy in Tripoli.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d48.summary: In this January 8, 1976 cable Secretary Kissinger told the U.S. Embassy in Tripoli that the U.S. was lifting limits on the size of the Libyan mission in Washington, in return for Libya having lifted the ceiling on U.S. diplomatic staff in Tripoli. The Department said it would not yet release Libya's C-130s or accept a Libyan ambassador, because Libya still opposed Middle East peace efforts.
tripoli_details: Libya's note of September 2, 1975 conveyed the lifting of the restriction on U.S. diplomatic staff at the U.S. Embassy in Tripoli.
The embassy was told to inform the Libyan Foreign Ministry orally of the decision.
The Department said it had not granted agrément for a Libyan ambassador.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d79.summary: In this January 28, 1977 cable the State Department reported delivering a protest to the Libyan chargé over an incident on January 27 in which two Libyan Mirage fighters harassed an unarmed U.S. Navy plane over international waters. The note said the Libyan jets came within 200 feet and lit the U.S. aircraft with fire control radar.
tripoli_details: The incident took place about 75 nautical miles north of Tripoli, while the U.S. aircraft never came closer than 53 nautical miles from Libyan territory.
The Libyan aircraft approached from the southeast and the American plane was at 13,500 feet.
The U.S. aircraft was illuminated with fire control radar from 10:32 until about 10:43 a.m. GMT.
The note was handed to Libyan Chargé Gashut, and the Embassy in Tripoli was asked to deliver a copy to the Libyan Foreign Ministry.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d102.summary: On June 22, 1979 Secretary Vance reported to President Carter on Under Secretary Newsom's June 16-18 mission to Libya. Newsom met Major Jallud and the Foreign Minister but not Qadhafi, whose mother had died, and found Libya willing to talk but angry about the refusal to supply 747 and C-130 aircraft.
tripoli_details: Qadhafi was unavailable, apparently because of his mother's death.
The U.S. had 2,500 Americans in Libya, oil imports of 700,000 barrels a day (10 percent of U.S. imports) and investments with replacement value of $2.5 billion.
Qadhafi received West German Foreign Minister Genscher June 18-20 and hoped to visit Bonn, Rome, Paris and London in July.
The memo said possible Libyan retaliation could include severing relations, offering naval facilities to the Soviets or nationalizing U.S. investments.
The U.S. had stopped the 747s after Libyans used 727s in operations in Uganda.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d119.summary: In this December 1974 cable the U.S. Embassy in Tunis reported Tunisia's request for military assistance to counter perceived threats from Libya and Algeria. The Tunisian Prime Minister said Libya was insisting on unity with Tunisia, that Soviet arms and '400 technicians' were flowing into Libya, and he cited Qadhafi's reported statement that unity would come in 1975 if necessary by force.
tripoli_details: The cable asked Embassy Tripoli to comment on a reported statement by Qadhafi that unity with Tunisia would be achieved in 1975.
It said the Tunisian government learned that Libya had informed Tunisians of the names of Libyans who would attend Tunisian maneuvers in the south.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d9.summary: In this May 30, 1977 cable the U.S. Embassy in Tripoli reported that a Libyan Foreign Affairs official summoned the chargé to complain that a U.S. naval unit at Gabes, Tunisia complicated the continental shelf dispute with Tunisia. The Libyan said Libya might be forced to invite a naval unit from a friendly country, which the embassy took to mean the Soviets.
tripoli_details: Under Secretary Atrash summoned the chargé on the morning of May 30, 1977.
Atrash said Foreign Secretary Turayki had hoped to go to Tunis but 'Tunisians had made it impossible for him to leave Tripoli.'
The chargé said a U.S. drilling rig was contracted by Libyan NOC and Reading & Bates contrary to U.S. advice, and that 6th Fleet visits to Tunisian ports were scheduled months in advance.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d113.summary: In this December 9, 1979 cable, U.S. Chargé Eagleton reported a three-hour talk in Tripoli with Ali Houdairi, Libya's chief in Washington, followed by a tour of the damaged embassy. Eagleton said elements of the Libyan government were involved in the December 2 attack from beginning to end and demanded Libya acknowledge responsibility for the lack of security.
tripoli_details: Eagleton toured the Embassy damaged in the December 2 attack.
He cited details such as tools supplied by the Popular Resistance office across the street and Embassy files removed to official Libyan vehicles and the Peoples Resistance building.
Houdairi saw Qadhafi on December 8, but Qadhafi declined to receive Eagleton, saying he never receives ambassadors, and said he would send a special emissary.
Eagleton warned that a proliferation of revolutionary committees eager to show zeal threatened the embassy.

frus-1981-88v24-d89.summary: This May 23, 1988 cable from the U.S. Embassy in Tunis reports Qadhafi's meeting with Tunisian President Ben Ali on the island of Jerba, which produced a communiqué listing seven accords. The accords covered free movement of persons and goods, a common identity card and joint projects including a Tripoli hospital.
tripoli_details: Joint projects listed included the Tripoli hospital, the Jbel Lakhdhar agricultural project and the Iron and Steel Consortium at Misrata.
Central Bank Governor Khelil said Tunisia benefited from sales to visiting Libyans and jobs for Tunisians in Libya.
The embassy noted the meeting came shortly before Ben Ali's expected visit to Tripoli.

frus-1981-88v24-d70.summary: In this June 12, 1986 cable the U.S. Ambassador in Rabat reported telling King Hassan that U.S.-Moroccan cooperation against Libya would be the centerpiece of his upcoming Washington visit. Hassan agreed Libya supported terrorism and said Qadhafi could turn on Morocco at any time, but wanted such talks kept very discreet.
tripoli_details: Hassan said Libya, along with Algeria, represented the greatest threat to Morocco.
He said the Oujda Accord with Libya had been designed to 'neutralize Qadhafi, not just to isolate him.'
The ambassador said Washington wanted an end to the Moroccan-Libyan relationship.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d40.summary: In this June 4, 1975 cable Kissinger instructed the U.S. Ambassador in Cairo to tell Sadat that the U.S. was inclined to accept Mohamed Yunis Khalifa as Libya's ambassador in Washington and raise the ceiling on Libyan embassy staff. It said there was no present intention to assign an ambassador to Tripoli.
tripoli_details: On April 15, 1975 the Libyan Government told the U.S. Chargé in Tripoli orally that the ceiling on U.S. Embassy personnel in Libya had been lifted.
The cable said the U.S. had not replaced Ambassador Palmer because he had not been received at levels appropriate for his rank and had very little contact with Libyans.
It said the larger Libyan embassy staff was needed to handle the large number of Libyan students in the U.S.

frus-1981-88v24-d22.summary: In this cable of July 1983, relayed to Chad, the U.S. Ambassador in Rabat reported King Hassan's account of Qadhafi's visit to Morocco. Hassan called Qadhafi erratic and 'schizophrenic' but intelligent, said no agreements were reached, and planned to send an envoy to Libya about diplomatic relations.
tripoli_details: Qadhafi came for a planned two-day visit and stayed four days.
Hassan said he planned to send a special envoy to Libya to explore setting up diplomatic relations with the Tripoli government.
Qadhafi told Hassan there were no Libyan troops in Chad.
Hassan said Qadhafi's female bodyguards glowered at guests over their weapons at formal dinners.

frus-1981-88v24-d76.summary: In this February 19, 1987 cable the U.S. Embassy in Tunis reported Prime Minister Baccouche's account of Qadhafi's February 5-7 visit to Tunis. Baccouche said Qadhafi behaved well, agreed that resolving the Western Sahara should come first, and Baccouche estimated 80 to 90 percent of Libyans were ready for a change of leadership.
tripoli_details: Ben Ali and Qadhafi agreed to eliminate visa requirements from February 15, but Libya was requiring each Tunisian traveler to carry TD200 in hard currency.
Only twelve Libyans had entered Tunisia because a Libyan exit visa could be obtained only by proven regime loyalists.
Tunisian Interior Minister Ammar visited Tripoli on February 16 to discuss entry rules.
Baccouche said Qadhafi seemed less energetic and aggressive than in the past.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d11.summary: In Telegram 460 of April 11, 1973 the U.S. Chargé in Tripoli, Harold Josif, urged Washington to reconsider the timing of resumed reconnaissance flights off Libya. He argued that more time should be allowed for diplomacy in Tripoli, given anti-American feeling after an Israeli raid on Beirut.
tripoli_details: The chargé said he was told on April 10 that the first reconnaissance flight had been scheduled for that day and then postponed 48 hours.
He noted that the Libyan government announced a popular demonstration in Tripoli at 1700 or 1800 local time on April 12, the hour of the burials in Beirut.
He wrote that differences with 'the rulers of Tripoli over transit rights go back to 1801.'
He said anti-American sentiment was the most extreme since the June 1967 War.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d15.summary: On April 19, 1973 CIA Director Schlesinger sent Kissinger a CIA paper on the problem posed by Qadhafi. The paper judged Qadhafi firmly in control with no successor in sight, unpopular on the planned merger with Egypt, and warned that hit-and-run raids to punish him would not bring him down.
tripoli_details: The paper said there were three Egyptian commando battalions in Libya and many Egyptians in the Libyan army and bureaucracy.
It said U.S. oil companies contributed 300 million dollars per year to the U.S. balance of payments.
It judged a popular reaction against Qadhafi's ouster unlikely if new military leaders cancelled the merger plans.

frus-1981-88v24-d13.summary: In this January 24, 1982 cable the U.S. Embassy in Algiers reported on Qadhafi's January 18-23 visit to Algeria, where he pushed for Algerian-Libyan-Syrian unity but largely failed. The embassy noted Algerian reserve: no dinner was held, there was little press coverage and no joint communiqué.
tripoli_details: A Tripoli radio broadcast of January 21 quoted Qadhafi proposing unity between Algeria, Libya and Syria.
Qadhafi met 800 Algerian students for a 'dialogue,' which was not reported in the press.
Qadhafi said the two parliaments would meet at the end of March and joint meetings would take place with the General People's Committee.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d78.summary: This June 16, 1971 airgram sent the U.S. Embassy in Libya the official Policy Planning Paper for Libya, to guide all embassy statements and plans. It describes U.S. interests as Libyan oil for NATO allies, an American community of about 3,900, and over one billion dollars of private oil investment, and calls for a low official profile.
tripoli_details: It calls for expanding the libraries of publications in Arabic and English at the USIS centers in Tripoli and Benghazi.
It lists the American community in Libya at approximately 3,900 and 450 Libyan students in the United States.
It says Libya's oil income would soon be $2 billion a year, and U.S. oil industry payments to the U.S. balance of payments were $828 million in 1969.

frus-1981-88v24-d69.summary: This April 17, 1986 memo from Deputy Assistant Secretary Raphel to Secretary Shultz reports what a Moroccan delegation saw in Tripoli after the U.S. air strikes. The Moroccans met a calm, uninjured Qadhafi in the Azizziya compound, and Qadhafi alleged his adopted daughter was killed and two sons injured.
tripoli_details: The Moroccan delegation visited Tripoli on April 16, stayed seven hours, and met Qadhafi for 15 to 20 minutes at his 'office' in the Azizziya compound.
Qadhafi's home was severely damaged but not destroyed, and windows in his 'office' were blown out.
Qadhafi alleged his 15-month-old adopted daughter was killed and two sons moderately injured.
The Moroccans were given a restricted, guided tour and saw damage to the French embassy and nearby private residences destroyed.
The delegation described an atmosphere of a 'state of war' and thought the Libyan public was rallying to Qadhafi.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d6.summary: In this April 16, 1977 cable the U.S. Ambassador in Cairo reported Egyptian Foreign Minister Fahmy's statement that Egypt had decided to topple Qadhafi. Fahmy said Egypt burned the Libyan Relations Office in Alexandria in retaliation for Libyan action against an Egyptian office in Benghazi, and complained the U.S. was 'soft' on Qadhafi.
tripoli_details: Fahmy said Libyan diplomats had been forbidden to leave Egypt until Egyptian officials in Libya were allowed to leave.
He said the border was not formally closed but tightly controlled.
Fahmy said Egypt would charge Qadhafi with plotting terrorist activities against embassies in some Arab countries.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d16.summary: This July 7, 1977 CIA intelligence cable reports that Egyptian President Sadat ordered Qadhafi removed, by covert action if possible or by military operation. Egypt planned an armored brigade incursion across northeastern Libya toward Benghazi, though Egyptian Military Intelligence doubted it would succeed.
tripoli_details: Sadat gave the order in about January 1977 and by late June was ninety percent convinced of the military option.
Egyptian Military Intelligence believed the brigade would not reach Benghazi in force and that Libyans would rally behind Qadhafi.
Egyptian intelligence confirmed Libya was reinforcing its eastern defenses with Soviet and Cuban military advisors.
The cable said Soviet signal ships anchored in the Gulf of Sallum might jam Egyptian communications.

frus-1981-88v24-d2.summary: In this January 29, 1981 cable the U.S. Embassy in Tunis reported on Libyan Foreign Secretary Turayki's visit to Tunisia. The meeting with Prime Minister Mzali was acrimonious, Bourguiba declined to receive Turayki, and Turayki defended Libya's role in Chad and denied that Libyan camps trained Tunisian dissidents.
tripoli_details: Turayki pushed for a follow-up visit to Tripoli by a Tunisian minister, probably Mezri Chekir.
He said Libyan camps merely processed papers of Tunisians who had crossed into Libya looking for work.
He said Libya had proposed Nigerian troops replace Libyan forces in Chad but Lagos refused.

frus-1981-88v24-d82.summary: In this October 8, 1987 cable the U.S. Embassy in Rabat said Morocco, Tunisia and Algeria were all dealing with Qadhafi for their own reasons, so the U.S. struggled to keep him isolated. The embassy argued that progress on the Western Sahara conflict was needed before friends would heed U.S. arguments on Libya.
tripoli_details: The embassy said Morocco did not object to Libyan-Tunisian and Libyan-Algerian rapprochement.
It noted the Arab African union with Libya was by then defunct.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d91.summary: On August 9, 1972 NSC staffer Harold Saunders sent Kissinger a memo on the U.S. relationship with Libya and its effect on American oil companies. He reported that Libya's Jallud had linked the companies' position to U.S. refusal to deliver 8 F-5 aircraft, that nationalization of three companies was rumored for September 1, and asked whether to release at least a couple of the planes.
tripoli_details: Reports said the government planned to nationalize three oil companies on September 1, the anniversary of the revolution.
In mid-June Jallud called in the heads of the oil companies and told them their position was jeopardized by U.S. arms policy.
CIA analysts judged the Minister of the Interior and security chief Al Houni, third in power after Qadhafi, led a moderating faction toward the oil companies.
The Libyans had ordered 8 C-130s through commercial channels for delivery the next year.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d14.summary: On April 17, 1973 NSC staffers Saunders and Kennedy told Kissinger that a U.S. reconnaissance flight off Libya went off without incident. They attached an options paper on how to respond if Libya attacked U.S. aircraft, ranging from diplomatic protest to withholding military spares and military action.
tripoli_details: The paper said the U.S. did not recognize Libya's restricted area within 100 nautical miles of Tripoli.
It noted about 3,000 U.S. citizens in Libya and U.S. investments in excess of $1 billion.
It listed military options such as authorizing hot pursuit into Libyan airspace and operating from an aircraft carrier outside the 12-mile limit.
It warned the U.S. should be prepared to evacuate U.S. citizens from Libya if a serious incident occurred.

frus-1981-88v24-d24.summary: This July 25, 1983 cable from the U.S. Embassy in Nouakchott reports Qadhafi's 45-hour visit to Mauritania, where officials were wary and the public relatively indifferent. The embassy said Qadhafi behaved politely, denied Libyan troops were in Chad, and made no startling revelations on the Western Sahara.
tripoli_details: Qadhafi arrived with an entourage of 200 aboard four aircraft and brought his own food, including lambs.
Mauritania has a sizeable contingent of Libyan secondary school teachers, whom Qadhafi met.
The embassy noted Qadhafi's 1981 visit had been a public relations disaster.

frus-1981-88v24-d61.summary: In this September 27, 1985 cable the U.S. Embassy in Tunis reported that Tunisia broke diplomatic relations with Libya for the first time, after expelling workers and letter bombs sent by Libyan diplomats. The embassy said Tunisia cited Libyan subversion, press campaigns, threats of force and airspace violations, and was now putting the U.S. up front as its supporter.
tripoli_details: Tunisia announced the break on the evening of September 26, 1985, citing 'irrefutable' proof of Libyan use of its diplomatic presence for terrorism, espionage and subversion.
In early August Libya expelled Tunisian workers; the embassy estimated only about 15,000 Tunisians remained in Libya and about 10,000 Libyan passport holders were in Tunisia.
In March a clandestine radio station had broadcast encouragement to Tunisians to kill Jews, which led Bourguiba to dismiss Libyan Foreign Minister Turayki from his office.
The embassy noted Tripoli had yet to react but had issued unconvincing denials of complicity in the letter bombs.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d50.summary: In this April 14, 1976 cable the State Department authorized the Embassy in Tripoli to deliver a diplomatic note assuring Libya that eight C-130 aircraft sold by Lockheed belong solely to the Libyan government. The cable also noted that Qadhafi and RCC member Muhayshi were trading accusations involving Lockheed payments.
tripoli_details: The note concerned eight C-130s under Lockheed contracts GLX-221 (September 13, 1972) and GLX-230 (November 27, 1972).
The Libyan Chargé in Washington asked Lockheed for information about Muhayshi and an Egyptian minister.
A related Tripoli cable of April 6 summarized a Qadhafi speech indicating Muhayashi had been recruited by 'international intelligence' and perhaps bribed by Lockheed.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d81.summary: In this February 12, 1977 cable the State Department instructed the Embassy in Tripoli to deliver a note rejecting Libya's claim of a prohibited zone over international waters, after the January 27 incident with a U.S. Navy plane. The U.S. said its plane stayed 53 nautical miles from the Libyan coast and was intercepted 75 nautical miles off Libyan shores.
tripoli_details: The note replied to a Libyan Foreign Ministry note dated February 7, 1977.
The U.S. said no nation could subject any part of the high seas or the airspace over it to its sovereignty.

frus-1981-88v24-d16.summary: In this July 30, 1982 cable the U.S. Embassy in Tunis reported Tunisian Secretary of State Mestiri's view that Tunisian-Libyan rapprochement was 'frozen' because Tunisia refused to attend the OAU summit in Tripoli. Mestiri said Tunisia was re-entering a 'state of confrontation' with Qadhafi.
tripoli_details: Essebsi and Economy Minister Lasram got nowhere when they visited Libya on July 19 to explore a deal on the continental shelf.
The embassy said Bourguiba was indignant at Qadhafi's failure to receive Tunisia's ministers earlier that month.
Qadhafi had warned that Tunisia's boycott of the OAU summit in Tripoli would harm bilateral cooperation.

frus-1981-88v24-d41.summary: This October 25, 1984 memo from DIA Director Lt. Gen. Williams to Defense Secretary Weinberger reports a meeting with the Moroccan Ambassador about Morocco's new treaty with Libya. The ambassador, who had served in Libya, said King Hassan thought dialogue better than confrontation and described Qadhafi as clever rather than crazy; Williams doubted the relationship would last.
tripoli_details: Ambassador Jorio said Libya in theory has no governmental structure, only committees, and does not recognize other countries' governmental institutions.
He said Qadhafi lives simply and sleeps in a barracks or a tent, and that 'There is no number two man in Libya.'
Williams noted Qadhafi's conduct that year in London and 'most likely the Red Sea.'

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d49.summary: On December 23, 1969 Assistant Secretary Newsom reported that the Embassy in Tripoli said agreement had been reached with Libya for U.S. withdrawal from Wheelus by June 30, 1970. The agreed minute was expected to be signed that evening, possibly as Nasser arrived in Tripoli.
tripoli_details: An agreed minute was expected to be signed at 8:00 p.m. Tripoli time on December 23, 1969.
Nasser's arrival in Tripoli as a guest was expected for a two-day visit and might reveal that about 1,000 Egyptian troops had been in Libya for about a week.
The British agreed to withdraw from their bases by March 31, 1970.
Newsom said Ambassador Palmer would ask Captain Jaluud, who led the Libyan negotiating team, to assure the base would not be transferred to any third country.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d12.summary: On April 12, 1973 Kissinger asked President Nixon to approve an armed-escorted U.S. reconnaissance flight off Libya, after Libyan aircraft fired at an American plane on 21 March. Kissinger weighed risks including danger to the 3,000 Americans in Libya, and Nixon approved.
tripoli_details: Libya had declared a 'restricted area' reaching 100 miles around its capital in 1972.
On 21 March two Libyan aircraft fired at and tried to force down a U.S. reconnaissance plane about 82 nautical miles off Libya.
Libya's planes were on 'strip alert' with air-to-air missiles, and there were indications Libya was seeking an incident as an excuse to break with the U.S.
The closest point of approach to Libya for the escorted flight was 75 nautical miles, with escort from an aircraft carrier.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d28.summary: In Telegram 1257 of September 30, 1973 the U.S. Chargé in Tripoli answered the Department's questions on the future of the embassy. He judged Libya had not decided to force the U.S. out and that accepting Arabic in passports would probably let the embassy keep operating, though under growing difficulty.
tripoli_details: The chargé suspected the RCC debated its response after a Libyan airliner was shot down in Sinai on February 21 (1973).
He wrote that few diplomats expected the planned unity with Egypt to go ahead.
Allies thought the U.S. had put up a 'magnificent but quixotic fight' on passports and feared a deadline for printing foreign passports in Arabic.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d28.summary: On February 21, 1978 Secretary Vance told President Carter that Chad and Libya had agreed to a ceasefire and to resume diplomatic relations, largely through Sudanese mediation. He judged the future uncertain and thought Libya might be showing reasonableness to an OAU ministerial conference then meeting in Tripoli.
tripoli_details: An OAU ministerial conference was convening in Tripoli.
The ceasefire followed the fall of Chad's last major northern garrison, Faya-Largeau, and Chad had lost 40 percent of its 5,000 man army killed or captured in three weeks.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d123.summary: In this January 17, 1980 cable the State Department sent U.S. Chargé Eagleton the text of a letter from President Carter to Qadhafi, to be delivered in Tripoli. Carter asked for safe conditions for U.S. representatives, regular access to senior Libyan decision makers, and Libyan help in opposing the Soviet move into Afghanistan.
tripoli_details: Eagleton was told to seek an early appointment with Qadhafi to deliver the message.
Carter asked Qadhafi to designate a close associate with whom the chief U.S. representative in Tripoli could remain in touch.
Carter welcomed Qadhafi's assurances about the safety of U.S. representatives.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d48.summary: In Telegram 3711 of December 13, 1969 U.S. Ambassador Palmer proposed a contingency public statement in case Libya exposed meetings between a U.S. officer and Lt. Col. Adam al-Hawwaz, the former Defense Minister arrested in an alleged counter-coup. Palmer noted that Qadhafi on TV said Hawwaz had admitted his role in plotting and that security personnel watched visitors to the Defense Ministry.
tripoli_details: An officer of the Embassy Branch Office in Benghazi met Hawwaz on December 2 and 4, 1969; Hawwaz asked whether the U.S. would give him a substantial sum of money.
The U.S. officer told Hawwaz the U.S. would give no assistance of any kind to him or any Libyan.
Qadhafi said on TV that the RCC was planning a thorough investigation and that trials were promised.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d62.summary: On July 2, 1970 Deputy Assistant Secretary Moore asked Acting Secretary Johnson to approve terminating outstanding U.S.-Libyan agreements left over from the monarchy. Moore argued that an amicable termination of the Wheelus, economic aid and military assistance agreements would give leverage and lay the basis for a 'post-Wheelus' relationship.
tripoli_details: The agreements included the 1954 Defense Facilities Agreement and the Economic Assistance Agreement, and Ambassador Palmer already had authority to sign the Wheelus termination.
Formal notes of termination were sent to Tripoli on July 4, 1970.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d17.summary: On May 10, 1973 Under Secretary Porter sent Secretary Rogers a review of U.S.-Libyan relations and proposed actions to avoid a break in diplomatic relations before the planned Libyan-Egyptian union. Topics included Arabic passports, a Lockheed C-130 maintenance contract, the expulsion of a U.S. political officer, oil talks and reconnaissance flights.
tripoli_details: Libya declared the Embassy's Political Officer, Charles Marthinsen, persona non grata, and the Embassy staff had been cut from 15 to 13.
Porter said Qadhafi might be goading the U.S. to break relations before the projected union with Egypt on September 1.
Lockheed's two-year C-130 contract, worth about $4,000,000, would include a clause allowing suspension if Libya merged with Egypt.
DOD had tentatively scheduled two reconnaissance flights off Libya in May.

frus-1981-88v24-d185.summary: This January 6, 1989 State Department cable reports an Algerian Ambassador's démarche about the January 4 shootdown of Libyan MiGs by U.S. forces and U.S. charges about Libya's chemical weapons plant at Rabta. A U.S. official called the shootdown a discrete, closed incident and said it was unrelated to the chemical weapons issue.
tripoli_details: The Algerian Ambassador asked about Libya's alleged offer, relayed by Italian Foreign Minister Andreotti on December 24, to allow inspection of the Rabta facility, which Libya said was only a pharmaceutical plant.
The U.S. official said the Federal Republic of Germany was investigating German firms' involvement in the Libyan chemical weapons effort.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d52.summary: This memo of February 1970 from Kissinger to President Nixon concerns the future U.S. relationship with the Libyan Air Force once Wheelus closed. The recommended approach was commercial maintenance by Norair, continued spares and limited pilot training, a five-person Air Force liaison unit in the embassy, and no commitment to ship eight remaining F-5s; Nixon approved.
tripoli_details: The U.S. Air Force at Wheelus had helped the Libyans start their own air force, and the U.S. delivered ten F-5 aircraft after 1967.
Libya had seven remaining F-5s, and the U.S. would maintain a liaison unit of five USAF people in the embassy.
The commercial sale of two C-130s was proceeding.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d60.summary: This June 12, 1970 memo reported the formal handover of Wheelus Air Force Base to Libya on June 11, 1970. The last 48 USAF personnel left for Germany, and Libya renamed the base 'Ukba ibn Nafia.'
tripoli_details: On June 11, 1970 the U.S. formally turned over Wheelus after an uninterrupted U.S. presence since World War II, in a ceremony attended by Acting Prime Minister Jaluud and Ambassador Palmer.
The property cost $77 million at initial construction and was valued at $43 million; over 4,000 airmen and dependents were withdrawn.
Libya renamed Wheelus 'Ukba ibn Nafia' after the 7th century Arab conqueror, saying it would be used 'to defend Arabism and humanity.'
The Libyan Air Force kept its headquarters at Wheelus and French technicians were expected there for Mirage deliveries.
Ambassador Palmer later boycotted the remaining events after the Libyan Air Force commander criticized Washington at the turnover ceremony.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d47.summary: In Telegram 925 of August 18, 1975 the U.S. Embassy in Tripoli reported a talk with the Libyan Foreign Ministry's Ambassador Shaaban about the U.S. reversal on the Northrop-Page contract. Shaaban complained U.S. responses were one-sided and warned that without better political ties, commercial and cultural links could suffer.
tripoli_details: Shaaban said the Libyan Ministry organized a program for U.S. Country Officer Jameson's visit and arranged for him to meet Acting Undersecretary Al-Atrash.
Shaaban said Libya could educate students elsewhere and had good relations with France and the USSR.
He admitted he could not say for certain why propaganda attacks on Sadat had stopped the week before, suggesting the RCC may have given an unofficial directive.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d57.summary: This memorandum records a December 2, 1976 meeting in Mexico City between Secretary Kissinger and Libyan Permanent Representative Kikhia. Kissinger urged Kikhia to confer with Scranton, get fresh instructions from Tripoli, and bring concrete ideas, while Kikhia asked if the plane (C-130) issue could be resolved in the context of general relations.
tripoli_details: Kissinger told Kikhia to get fresh instructions from Tripoli.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d115.summary: In this December 14, 1979 cable, U.S. Chargé Eagleton relayed Political Officer Hooper's five premises on the basis for a continuing U.S. diplomatic relationship with Libya, after the embassy attack. They said Qadhafi was prone to lie, that oil and educational ties were largely self-sustaining, and that political dialogue would founder while Qadhafi remained in power.
tripoli_details: The cable said visa services for Libyan students could be provided by other U.S. embassies in Europe and the Middle East.
It said American oil company officials found a U.S. diplomatic presence in Tripoli convenient but not essential.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d126.summary: On March 11, 1980 the State Department's Tarnoff told Brzezinski that after the Gafsa raid and the February 4 attack on the French Embassy in Tripoli, the U.S. had withdrawn its chargé and reduced the embassy staff to two. Chargé Eagleton would return about March 13 to pack up and say farewell, with a small junior staff of five to remain.
tripoli_details: The French Embassy in Tripoli was attacked on February 4, 1980.
Eagleton would return to Tripoli around March 13 to pack up and pay farewell calls on American community leaders, diplomatic colleagues and Libyan officials.
A small, relatively junior staff of five would stay in Tripoli to provide basic services and some political and economic reporting.

frus-1981-88v24-d60.summary: In this September 12, 1985 cable the U.S. Embassy in Tunis assessed Tunisia's confrontation with Libya after Morocco's Oujda accord with Qadhafi. The embassy said Tunisia felt isolated and militarily weak, was coordinating more with Algeria, and might be planning clandestine options against Qadhafi.
tripoli_details: The embassy said Tunisian military planning included retaliation for a commando-type operation.
A Tunisian ambassador in Algiers had hinted at Algero-Tunisian planning for conflict with Libya and the removal of Qadhafi.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d120.summary: In Telegram 1349 of December 16, 1974 the U.S. Embassy in Tripoli answered a Tunis cable about Tunisian fears of Libya. The embassy said it had seen no Qadhafi statement threatening unity with Tunisia by force in 1975, and judged Tunisia had more to fear from Libyan subversion than military attack.
tripoli_details: The embassy quoted Qadhafi's statement at the Libya ASU Congress on November 6 that Arab unity could not be imposed by force and 'there is no question of this now.'
It said it had no information confirming building of airstrips along the Tunisian border.
It noted SRF reports of Libyan propaganda teams and other Libyan-backed subversives in Tunisia.

frus-1981-88v24-d155.summary: In this December 17, 1985 letter Vice President Bush told Algerian President Bendjedid that the U.S. shared his view of Qadhafi's malevolent designs and cited a Libyan role in the recent Egypt Air hijacking. Bush warned of a Libyan buildup in northern Chad, Libyan designs on Sudan and possible Soviet SA-5 missile deliveries, and urged Bendjedid to send a strong message when he met Qadhafi.
tripoli_details: Bush cited well-documented evidence of Libyan plots against American government installations in Khartoum.
He said the U.S. credited reports of a significant buildup of Libyan forces in northern Chad, including the Aozou strip.
He cited reports that the Soviets had agreed to major new arms deliveries to Libya, possibly including SA-5 missiles.
