frus-1969-76ve09p1-d8.summary: In Telegram 51869 of March 29, 1973 the State Department sent the Embassy in Tripoli the text of a protest note over the March 21 attack by Libyan aircraft on an unarmed U.S. military transport over the high seas. The note demanded an investigation and said the U.S. would hold Libya fully accountable for future incidents.
tripoli_details: The note was to be presented to the Libyan Ministry of Foreign Affairs by the Embassy in Tripoli.
The Department called in the Libyan Chargé to present a parallel note in Washington.
The Embassy was told to reject any Libyan justification based on the restricted-area declaration HLR 22.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d9.summary: On April 5, 1973 Deputy Defense Secretary Clements sent Kissinger options for responding to the March 21 Libyan attempt to shoot down a U.S. C-130. The four options ranged from diplomatic protest to sending an escorted aircraft, and Clements recommended Option 3 or 4.
tripoli_details: The letter said Libya's restricted area extends within 100 nautical miles of Tripoli and the U.S. did not recognize it.
It noted about 3,000 U.S. citizens and over $1 billion of U.S. investments in Libya.
It warned that escalation could put U.S. lives in Libya and elsewhere at increased risk from fedayeen reprisals.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d20.summary: This June 22, 1973 memo from Assistant Secretary Newsom explains why the U.S. kept refusing Libya's demand that U.S. passports carry an Arabic translation. Libya was refusing entry to U.S. government employees, so the embassy could not rotate its staff, but Newsom advised holding firm, hoping the planned merger with Egypt would solve it.
tripoli_details: Libya would not allow any U.S. government employees to enter, and British, Swiss, German and Venezuelan diplomats had the same problem.
U.S. businessmen and families were generally being admitted without major problems.
Newsom noted Libya would admit foreigners it needed, such as petroleum engineers, and expel those it did not want.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d35.summary: In Telegram 1115 of October 10, 1974 the U.S. Chargé in Tripoli, Stein, gave his view of Libyan overtures after Finance Minister Rajab met Under Secretary Sisco. He thought the main Libyan aim was approval to export their C-130s, and noted that only RCC members could decide matters, so a Foreign Ministry reorganization with RCC Major Al-Huni as minister might improve the channel.
tripoli_details: He said RCC members greet visiting dignitaries but are normally not available to resident diplomats in Tripoli.
He said a reorganization of the Foreign Ministry might be announced within a week, possibly with Major Abdul Muneim Al-Huni as foreign minister.
He suggested Wiley or Saunders make a quiet visit to Tripoli to begin substantive talks.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d36.summary: In Telegram 38 of January 10, 1975 the U.S. Embassy in Tripoli reported a Libyan protest note alleging Sixth Fleet aircraft had pursued an Algerian civilian airliner about 60 miles north of Misrata. The Libyan official softened the note's tone, mentioning positive steps such as lifting the oil embargo.
tripoli_details: The Libyan Foreign Ministry called in the embassy on the afternoon of January 10, and Najib Shaybani delivered the note in a sealed envelope in a 20-minute meeting held in Arabic.
The note said an American carrier was 60 miles north of Misrata and its aircraft came within 10 miles of land, which Libya called 'complete air piracy.'
Shaybani said Libya had lifted the oil embargo and decided to buy a Triga III reactor from General Atomic, and oil shipments were going to the U.S.
The embassy said Libyan military aircraft continued to be active over Tripoli and recommended the naval unit avoid provocative operations.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d90.summary: This July 8, 1977 State Department cable records a June 29 conversation between Deputy Assistant Secretary Veliotes and Libyan Chargé Gashut. Gashut asked for an exchange of ambassadors and release of the C-130s, while Veliotes said Libya's rejectionist policy and support for terrorism blocked progress and no higher-level dialogue was useful then.
tripoli_details: Gashut was returning to Libya for consultation and leave and said he would discuss U.S. relations with his Foreign Minister.
Veliotes cited the Rome airport massacre as an unacceptable terrorist act.
Gashut said Libya's goal was a secular democratic state in Palestine where Jews present before 1947 could remain.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d108.summary: This December 2, 1979 State Department situation report, sent to all posts, describes the attack that day on the U.S. Embassy in Tripoli by a mob of several hundred young men. Staff escaped unharmed to the British Embassy, the Chancery was set on fire, and Chargé Eagleton protested to Libyan Foreign Secretary Turayki.
tripoli_details: The Embassy was attacked about 10:00 a.m. on Sunday, December 2, 1979 by a mob of several hundred men aged 18 to 25 shouting anti-American slogans.

The mob breached the Embassy about 11:10 a.m. through a second floor balcony, and staff retreated to the third floor vault and left via a trap door about 11:15 a.m. to walk to the British Embassy, about 15 minutes away.
The mob arrived at the time of an anti-American, pro-Iranian rally of several thousand people at Green Square, about a mile from the Embassy.
Most members of the mob wore military fatigues, which had become standard clothing for students and others in Tripoli.
Fires set in the Chancery were extinguished by the local fire department; the first floor consular and economic/commercial areas suffered extensive fire and water damage.
At 4:00 p.m. Libyan police were placed in front and rear of the chargé's residence, and the Embassy was reoccupied about 7:00 p.m.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d52.summary: On July 2, 1980 NSC staffer Gary Sick told Aaron that Libya watchers generally agreed an assassination attempt on Qadhafi occurred in April, probably wounding his arm. Sick also worried that Egyptian troop movements in the Western Desert might signal a Sadat attack on Libya.
tripoli_details: Sick said killings of Libyans overseas began in March with a murder in Rome and may have prompted the attempt on Qadhafi.
He cited Qadhafi's assassination squads, mismanagement of the economy, devastated military morale and 'increasingly routine torture in Libyan prisons' as grievances.
He wrote that Qadhafi might have made a quick visit to Yugoslavia for medical treatment.

frus-1981-88v24-d32.summary: In this March 30, 1984 cable the State Department told the Embassy in Rabat to press Morocco on its rapprochement with Libya. It cited rising Libyan aggressiveness, including the London and Omdurman bombings, and said Morocco was paying a rising price in support on the Saharan issue.
tripoli_details: The Department said Libyan machinations could lead to actions targeting Americans, such as AWACS in Sudan, or NATO installations as at Comiso.
It listed Libyan efforts to absorb northern Chad, attacks on Sudan and Jordan, threats toward Egypt and attempts on Qadhafi's opponents abroad, as in the London bombings.

frus-1981-88v24-d37.summary: This August 14, 1984 cable from the U.S. Embassy in Rabat reports the August 13 meeting at Oujda between King Hassan and Qadhafi, which produced a treaty creating a union of states between Morocco and Libya. The embassy saw it as Hassan's bid to bolster Morocco against Algeria on the Western Sahara and as Qadhafi's means to reduce Libya's isolation.
tripoli_details: After the Oujda meeting Qadhafi went to Algiers and on August 14 to Tunis, accompanied by Moroccan Royal Counselor Guedira.
The embassy noted the treaty was handled in great secrecy and senior Moroccan ministers denied anything special was going on.
It speculated that the bait for Hassan may have been a promised Libyan fix for Morocco's cash flow problems.

frus-1981-88v24-d184.summary: In this December 26, 1988 cable the U.S. Ambassador in Algiers reported Algerian President Bendjedid urging a 'prudent and measured' response, rather than another military action against Libya, over its chemical weapons capability. Bendjedid said Jallud visited Algeria December 25 and that Algeria stood ready to press Libya diplomatically.
tripoli_details: Bendjedid said he raised the chemical weapons problem with Abd as-Salam Jallud during Jallud's visit on December 25.
The ambassador noted some Algerians and diplomats wanted to believe the Libyan chemical plant was only pharmaceutical.
The U.S. had just briefed Algerian Defense and Foreign Ministries on Libya's chemical weapons capability.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d57.summary: This May 9, 1970 joint State-Defense cable gave Ambassador Palmer instructions on the future U.S. relationship with the Libyan Air Force. The U.S. decided to defer a decision on delivering eight more F-5s while continuing pilot training and limited ammunition sales.
tripoli_details: The cable said the eight F-5s were expected to be ready for delivery in January and February 1971 but no action had been taken to divert them.
The U.S. was prepared to accept five Libyan pilots for training from late May 1970, with flying training beginning in October.
Palmer was to say that after the U.S. agreed to leave Wheelus, it had instead seen moves against the official and private American community.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d80.summary: This December 7, 1971 State Department memo reports that Libya announced the nationalization of British Petroleum's Libyan subsidiary that day. The memo suggested anger at Britain over Iran's seizure of Persian Gulf islands as one possible motive and noted a new company, the Arabian Gulf Prospecting Company, would take over BP's assets.
tripoli_details: Libyan Radio and Libyan News Agency announced the nationalization on December 7, 1971.
BP produced 200,000 barrels per day in Libya and operated the joint concession with Nelson Bunker Hunt.
The British Embassy in Tripoli feared on December 4 that Libya might take drastic action, including breaking relations.
Unconfirmed reports said Libya was transferring funds out of London, where its funds probably exceeded $2 billion.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d41.summary: In Telegram 5640 of June 7, 1975 the U.S. Ambassador in Cairo reported telling Egyptian Foreign Minister Fahmy of the U.S. plan to accept a Libyan ambassador. Sadat's reaction was distinctly negative, as he saw it as endorsing Libya's Soviet arms deal and a slap at him.
tripoli_details: The Libyan note of April 14 requested agrément for Khalifa as Ambassador to the U.S., and on April 15 Libya lifted the ceiling on U.S. Embassy personnel in Libya.
Fahmy said Qadhafi's recent attacks on Sadat for attending the Salzburg Summit and reopening the Suez Canal had become shriller.
The U.S. then postponed the matter indefinitely.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d99.summary: This March 9, 1979 informal letter from State Department official James Bishop to Chargé Eagleton in Tripoli discusses the controversy over selling Boeing 747s to Libya and Libyan support for Idi Amin. Bishop said Newsom was astonished to learn that the U.S. was still delivering Chinook helicopters to Libya, which Libyans were using to train Palestinian pilots.
tripoli_details: Bishop noted that Libya's support for Amin had damaged its image and prompted press and congressional inquiries.
He said Muntasir's family had returned to Tripoli except a brother, and Muntasir was receiving out-patient treatment but was reportedly far from well.
He mentioned an interesting story about Libya's lost TU-22.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d141.summary: This October 21, 1980 State Department cable updates posts on a feared renewal of the Libyan assassination campaign, after the October 14 attack on Libyan graduate student Faisal Zagallai at Colorado State University. Libya's news agency said a member of the 'World Revolutionary Committee' did it, while the People's Bureau denied government involvement, and the U.S. demanded an explanation within 48 hours.
tripoli_details: JANA claimed the student was 'an agent and spy for American intelligence.'
The Libyan People's Bureau responded on October 20 that its answer came from Tripoli and represented the official position of the Jamahiriya.
The Department did not give the denial any real credibility.

frus-1981-88v24-d366.summary: This memorandum records a September 9, 1988 farewell meeting between General Colin Powell and outgoing Tunisian Ambassador Ben Yahia. Ben Yahia said there was 'fermentation' inside Libya, that one-third of Libyans had visited Tunisia since the border opened in 1987, and that Tunisia sought regional containment of Qadhafi.
tripoli_details: Ben Yahia said that since Tunisia opened its borders with Libya in 1987, fully one-third of the Libyan population had visited Tunisia.
He said Qadhafi's partial relaxation of internal controls had given Libyans a glimpse of more open societies.
Powell said the U.S. was concerned about Libya's chemical weapons program and support for terrorists.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d46.summary: In Telegram 3684 of December 11, 1969 Ambassador Palmer reported an abortive coup against Libya's new military regime, announced on Libyan radio the evening of December 10. Radio said the Defense and Interior ministers were involved, and Qadhafi hinted at foreign hands, implicitly the US and UK, though the embassy found the evidence skimpy.
tripoli_details: Libyan radio announced at about 1815 hours on December 10 that 'reactionaries and opportunists acting for imperialism' failed in an 'abortive plot.'
At 2200 hours radio named Minister of Defense Adam al-Hawwaz and Interior Minister Musa Ahmad al-Hasi as the only cabinet ministers involved, both under arrest.
A tour of Tripoli between 2030 and 2130 found no signs of anxiety, with police at normal posts and a support demonstration at the radio station featuring a huge picture of Qadhafi.

At 0830 on December 11 heavily armed troops were posted around the American, British, Italian and Lebanese embassies, with fifteen troops at the American Embassy and armored cars (Saladin and Ferret) nearby at 1000.
Qadhafi said Hawwaz had been prevented from committing suicide after his arrest, and that a court martial of military perpetrators would be held.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d47.summary: On December 11, 1969 NSC staffer Saunders sent Kissinger proposed negotiating instructions for Ambassador Palmer for the Wheelus Base talks starting the next Monday. The strategy was to avoid appearing to submit quickly, expect Libya to demand a firm withdrawal date first, and avoid strengthening pro-Egyptian elements before an Arab summit in Tripoli.
tripoli_details: The paper mentioned an Arab Summit or mini-Summit to follow in Tripoli.
It said the Libyan political situation was unstable and susceptible to change in unpredictable directions.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d66.summary: These minutes of an August 18, 1970 high-level meeting (memorandum for the record, with Kissinger, Mitchell, Packard, Helms and others) open with Ambassador Palmer's view of Libya. Palmer said the young regime seemed solidly established, anti-foreign feeling had begun to diminish, and the Soviet arms deal was cash-only without Soviet technicians so far.
tripoli_details: Palmer described the ruling officers as aged 24 to 28, the oldest 28 and the youngest 24.
He said planned oil cutbacks were really for conservation, to spin out the estimated 18-year life of the oil supply.
He said most Libyan students seeking education outside the Arab world would go to the United States, and officials worried about radicalization of foreign students.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d70.summary: In this February 23, 1971 CIA memo, Critchfield told the Director of Current Intelligence that Libya might be approaching a critical point. He listed judgments including that Qaddafi was taking personal control, Sadat may consider unseating him with Jallud as candidate, and the oil companies and Libya were far apart in negotiations.
tripoli_details: He wrote that he had seen no embassy reporting that Jallud had been downgraded while the relatively unknown Sulieman Qaradha and Al Huni were dominant in foreign policy.
He noted the British, Germans, Italians, Egyptians, Israelis, Libyan exiles and Soviets all had interests in Libya not congruent with the U.S.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d83.summary: In this December 22, 1971 letter Ambassador Palmer complained to Assistant Secretary Newsom that the Department had left him for about 18 months without a credible explanation for its 'no decision' on delivering the F-5 aircraft. He said he had lost the initiative with Libyan officials and would have to repeat the 'sorry charade' when pressed.
tripoli_details: Palmer referred to repeated approaches from a Libyan official named Yunis and other RCC members for an answer on the aircraft.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d38.summary: In Telegram 442 of April 15, 1975 the U.S. Embassy in Tripoli reported that Libya's Ahmad al-Atrash told the chargé on April 14 that Libya was removing the 1972 numerical ceiling on U.S. Embassy personnel. The embassy suggested lifting the ceiling on Libya's Washington embassy in return, but cautioned against an exchange of ambassadors.
tripoli_details: Al-Atrash called the chargé to the Foreign Ministry on April 14 and said the ceiling imposed in 1972 was removed by RCC decision, not to be made public or put in writing.
Al-Atrash gave the number of Libyan students in the U.S. as 1500 and suggested the U.S. might reopen its consulate in Benghazi, closed in 1972.
The embassy had a staff of seven officers in Tripoli.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d133.summary: These July 25, 1980 notes record a meeting in Brzezinski's office to prepare him for congressional hearings about his contacts with Libyan representatives and Billy Carter, the President's brother. They list chronologies to assemble, including Libya's reaction to the Tehran hostage-taking, and advice on how to testify.
tripoli_details: The notes mention a Qadhafi message to Khomeini and a Qadhafi interview saying relations would change.
They state that on December 12, 1979 the U.S.-Libyan relationship was very fragile.

frus-1981-88v24-d62.summary: This October 10, 1985 interagency intelligence assessment, 'Moroccan-Libyan Union: One Year Later,' judges the union serves both partners but costs King Hassan far more. Analysts said Hassan had received around $150 million in aid and that Qadhafi gained international standing and Moroccan goods easing consumer shortages in Libya.
tripoli_details: The assessment said a crippling shortage of essential consumer goods in Libya had prompted unprecedented criticism of Qadhafi's policies.
It said Qadhafi hoped to use Morocco as a conduit for restricted US equipment and spare parts, particularly for Libyan aircraft.
It judged Morocco was no longer a center of Libyan dissident activity.

frus-1981-88v24-d348.summary: This January 28, 1987 State Department cable reports Vice President Bush's January 23 meeting with Tunisian Ambassador Ben Yahia. He said Tunisia would not normalize relations with Libya without compensation for expelled workers and $200 million of seized assets, and welcomed Qadhafi's defeats in Chad.
tripoli_details: Ben Yahia said Tunisia demanded Libyan compensation for expelled Tunisian workers and for $200 million in seized assets.
He said Hassan had told Tunisia that Morocco's break with Libya was final.
He said U.S.-Tunisian joint contingency planning would assure Tunisia's security in the event of Libyan aggression.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d51.summary: In Telegram 169 of January 26, 1970 Ambassador Palmer reported meeting Qadhafi on military programs as Wheelus was being evacuated. Qadhafi said the lack of ammunition for F-5s was an obstacle and Palmer stressed new arrangements were needed for the Libyan Air Force once Wheelus closed.
tripoli_details: Qadhafi asked Palmer how the evacuation was proceeding.
Qadhafi asked Palmer to call again at 2000 local time at the Azizia barracks, after the Chief of Staff waited to see him the day before.
The local press did not report Palmer's call on Qadhafi.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d58.summary: This May 27, 1970 State Department intelligence brief asks whether Libya will move against the oil companies. It judged Qadhafi unlikely to nationalize the entire industry in the next few weeks, especially before U.S. forces fully left Wheelus in mid-June, but likely to harass individual companies such as Occidental.
tripoli_details: The brief said Qadhafi's government had recently launched an inter-Arab initiative with its own plan for an Arab-Israeli settlement.
It noted production limitations imposed on Occidental and that chief oil negotiator Mahmud Maghrabi believed some companies had engaged in corruption under the monarchy.
It said complete evacuation of American forces from Wheelus Air Base was scheduled for mid-June.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d49.summary: In this April 6, 1976 cable the State Department sent Chargé Carle in Tripoli the text of a Libyan diplomatic note asking for details of bribes paid in the Lockheed C-130 deal and assurances the planes would not go to Egypt. The Department noted Qadhafi's derogatory speeches and discussed how to respond.
tripoli_details: The Libyan note presented April 1, 1976 by Second Secretary Gaddour referred to a report by a Congressional committee headed by Senator Frank Church.
The Department cited a March 30 speech by Qadhafi as an example of derogatory references to the U.S.
Congress approved the sale of six C-130s to Egypt in April 1976.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d105.summary: On August 14, 1979 NSC staffer Rutherford Poats assessed a CIA report that Qadhafi might nationalize remaining U.S. oil interests in Libya on September 1. State discounted the report, and Poats weighed whether to appease Libya on the C-130 or 747 aircraft issue, noting Qadhafi had never acted irrationally on oil.
tripoli_details: The report suggested Qadhafi might nationalize on September 1, an anniversary of the revolution.
The memo noted Qadhafi previously expelled BP, Shell, Amoseas (Caltex) and Atlantic Richfield.
It named Oil Minister Ezzedin Mabrouk as a cooler head who understands the companies' marketing value.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d107.summary: In this October 10, 1979 diplomatic note the U.S. told Libya it would designate Libya's diplomatic office in Washington as the People's Bureau of the Diplomatic Mission of the Libyan Arab Jamahiriya. It asked for clarification of the status of the People's Committee members and for an official spokesman.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d138.summary: This September 19, 1980 CIA memorandum, 'Libya's Qadhafi: Seeking Significance Through Confrontation,' judged that the martyrdom theme in his speeches reflected a dangerous state of mind. Analysts linked it to his call for merger with Syria, calling it 'the resolution of death,' and to a year of failures.
tripoli_details: The memo said Qadhafi told his people to be prepared to die rather than submit, and that he would become a fedayeen and join the PLO if he could not persuade them.
It listed his failures: being pushed out of the limelight by the Egyptian-Israeli peace talks and Afghanistan, the failure in Uganda and the break with Fatah.
It said growing dissidence existed within Libya.

frus-1981-88v24-d229.summary: In this September 18, 1984 cable the U.S. Ambassador in Rabat reported King Hassan's explanation of why he signed the union with Libya: Morocco had been diplomatically isolated and he saw an opening. Hassan said he was working to turn Qadhafi into an 'oppositionist' rather than a terrorist and announced French-Libyan troop disengagement from Chad would take place between September 25 and November 1.
tripoli_details: Hassan said he would send Royal Counselor Guedira to Tripoli the following Monday to work out the structure of the union.
Hassan said Mitterrand's brother was persuaded to visit Libya, which helped lead to the French-Libyan agreement on troop withdrawal from Chad.
He said Arafat had asked him to reconcile him with Qadhafi.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d5.summary: This April 2, 1977 State Department cable reports Assistant Secretary Atherton's April 1 meeting with Tunisia's Ambassador Hedda on the Libyan-Tunisian continental shelf dispute. Atherton promised U.S. help in the Security Council if needed and consultation with France and Italy, but no assurance of more military aid.
tripoli_details: Hedda reported Qadhafi's threat to Tunisian Foreign Minister Chatty in Tripoli the previous week.
The Italian rig Scarabeo had apparently moved east out of the disputed area.
The cable noted Qadhafi was backtracking on the August 1976 agreement to submit the dispute to the Hague and demanding that operations in the Isis field be suspended.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d128.summary: This May 3, 1980 State Department cable reports the May 2 expulsion of four members of the Libyan People's Bureau in Washington for intimidating Libyan students in the United States. The U.S. cited the FBI investigation and murders of Libyans in London and Rome and warned the Bureau's status was in jeopardy.
tripoli_details: The four expelled were Nuri Swedan, Ali Ramram, Mohammad Gamudi and Abdula Zbedi, given 72 hours to leave.
The U.S. had declared two other People's Bureau diplomats persona non grata on April 6.
The note cited public statements by Libyan leaders calling for 'elimination' of opposition and the murders of two Libyans in London and two in Rome.

frus-1981-88v24-d81.summary: This August 21, 1987 State Department cable gave the Embassy in Tunis talking points against Tunisian rapprochement with Libya and against admitting Libya to the Maghreb friendship agreement. It said Qadhafi remained unreliable, aggressive in Chad and supportive of terrorism, and that Tunisia should insist on compensation for expelled workers.
tripoli_details: The Department said normalization should depend on compensation for expelled workers, a reduction of Libyan military presence along the border, and closing of dissident camps.
It said Libya faced a military confrontation with Chad supported by France and the U.S.

frus-1981-88v24-d86.summary: In this February 11, 1988 cable the U.S. Embassy in Rabat reported Moroccan reaction to Qadhafi's meetings with Tunisia's Ben Ali, Algeria's Bendjedid and Polisario leader Abdelaziz. Morocco was annoyed but silent officially, and noted Qadhafi said he had not resumed military aid to the Polisario.
tripoli_details: Qadhafi met Ben Ali at Sakiet and Bendjedid and Abdelaziz at Annaba in early February 1988.
In a February 9 AFP interview Qadhafi said Libya was furnishing only humanitarian assistance to the Polisario.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d75.summary: On May 8, 1971 Deputy Assistant Secretary Moore asked Secretary Rogers to approve telling Libya the U.S. would not deliver the remaining eight F-5 aircraft, invoking the contract's changed circumstances clause. Moore expected strong Libyan unhappiness but not a break in relations, and DOD dissented, preferring delay.
tripoli_details: Ambassador Palmer needed a decision before returning to Tripoli at the end of May, at least three months before the September 1 plebiscite on the Federation of Arab Republics.
The memo predicted Libya might obtain aircraft from the Soviets using the refusal as an excuse.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d18.summary: This May 22, 1973 memo from the 40 Committee concerns a CIA proposal to use President Mobutu of Zaire to counter Qadhafi's influence in Black Africa. State reconsidered its negative vote and accepted only a limited effort to generate anti-terrorism sentiment at the OAU, with limited financial support.
tripoli_details: The CIA argued that Qadhafi was pressuring African states to support Libyan policies inimical to the U.S. and that failure to oppose it could lead to proliferation of PLO offices.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d37.summary: In this January 14, 1975 cable Kissinger instructed the Embassy in Tripoli to deliver a reply to Libya's January 10 protest about U.S. aircraft. The U.S. said its aircraft never came closer than 25 nautical miles to the Libyan coast, did not pursue civilian planes, and were on routine missions, while saying the U.S. was ready to continue the dialogue.
tripoli_details: The Libyan note of January 10 concerned flights of Sixth Fleet aircraft near Misrata.
The embassy delivered the note to the Foreign Ministry on the morning of January 15.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d116.summary: These NSC staff notes from late 1979 record Special Coordination Committee discussions after the December 2 attack on the U.S. Embassy in Tripoli. Officials debated suspending or breaking relations, and by December 7 the U.S. was cutting embassy staff from 11 to 6 while Libya agreed to pay compensation but not full responsibility.
tripoli_details: On December 3 the SCC agreed to suspend relations with Libya, with Vance favoring suspension and establishment of an interests section.
On December 5 Warren Christopher said the plan was to suspend relations and reduce representation to an Interests Section, probably with the UK as host power.
On December 6 oil companies asked that some U.S. personnel stay in Libya; five people would remain.
On December 7 Christopher said Libya had sent two responses promising compensation but not taking full responsibility, and the staff was being cut from 11 to 6.

frus-1981-88v24-d14.summary: This memo of May 1982 records a CIA Director's meeting with Tunisian Prime Minister Mzali, who called Tunisian-Libyan normalization superficial and believed Qadhafi aimed to lower Tunisia's guard. Mzali said about 30,000 Tunisians visited Libya after Qadhafi's visit and returned shocked by the economic disorder there.
tripoli_details: Mzali said some 30,000 Tunisians had visited Libya since Qadhafi's visit, and almost all returned shocked by the economic disorder.
He said Qadhafi viewed the joint meetings as some form of union.

frus-1981-88v24-d341.summary: This Top Secret April 14, 1986 cable from Secretary Shultz told the U.S. Chargé in Tunis that the President had directed U.S. military forces to attack terrorist-related targets in Libya very soon. It supplied talking points to alert host governments after 2359 GMT on April 14, saying the U.S. had confirmation of Libyan-sponsored activity in Berlin and Paris and was not targeting civilians.
tripoli_details: The attacks would use land- and sea-based U.S. military aircraft against terrorist-related targets, command and control functions and logistics support in Libya.

The U.S. said it had information Libya was planning operations against U.S. citizens in twelve other countries, including Sudan, West Germany, Turkey, Syria, Spain, the Central African Republic and Kenya.
The talking points said the U.S. was not targeting civilians, economic facilities or regular military troop concentrations.

frus-1981-88v24-d256.summary: This April 22, 1986 cable from the U.S. Embassy in Rabat reports Moroccan reaction to the April 15 U.S. attack on Libya. The embassy said opposition parties complained the government had watered down parliamentary resolutions and police cracked down on protests, while Hassan wanted to keep ties with the U.S.
tripoli_details: The embassy said Communist daily Al Bayane gave banner headlines to a Washington Post report alleging the April 15 attack sought the death of Colonel Qadhafi.
King Hassan's April 15 letter to Qadhafi contained no condemnation of the U.S. action.
Interior Ministry officials suspected known Libyan contacts were the most active in fomenting protest in Morocco.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d42.summary: In Telegram 1134 of October 30, 1969 the U.S. consulate office in Benghazi reported that Libyan Foreign Minister Buwaysiir handed Ambassador Palmer a note calling for urgent discussions on evacuating the U.S. base at Wheelus. The minister said bases hurt relations and cited two cases in which U.S. employees smuggled Libyans out of the country.
tripoli_details: Palmer met the Foreign Minister in Benghazi on October 30, 1969, because Libyan ministries were spread across several cities.
The Foreign Minister had presented a similar note to the British Ambassador the day before.
The two 'exfiltration' cases were incidents in which U.S. employees at Wheelus smuggled two Libyans out of the country.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d55.summary: In Telegram 724 of April 13, 1970 Ambassador Palmer reported evidence that Libya's ruling council was debating whether to write off relations with the United States. One faction called the U.S. a 'lost cause,' while Foreign Ministry officials and others argued against a hasty decision.
tripoli_details: Former Prime Minister Mahmud Maghrabi told a visiting professor he had become a close adviser to Qadhafi and had sat on the platform during speeches at Tobruk, Derna and Baida.
The acting Libyan Air Force commander pressed the embassy on April 11 for definitive U.S. intentions on the air force.
Under Secretary Mansur Kikhya said the Foreign Ministry staff were in 'up-hill last ditch efforts' to convince the council to keep working with the U.S.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d81.summary: In this December 15, 1971 letter Secretary of State Rogers told Secretary of Defense Laird he would not allow the Spanish firm CASA to sell five F-5s to Libya. He cited Qadhafi's erratic behavior, including the December 7 nationalization of BP, and Section 9 of the Foreign Military Sales Act.
tripoli_details: Rogers wrote that Libyan funds supported the Fedayeen and that there were confirmed reports of Libyan commandos arriving in Syria.
He noted that Libya had supported the coup in Morocco and was causing difficulties for Chad and Eritrea.
He acknowledged it was a problem for Ambassador Palmer to keep telling the Libyans the sale remained under review.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d82.summary: This December 18, 1971 information memorandum to Secretary Rogers explains why the U.S. agreed to quietly support British demarches after Libya nationalized British Petroleum's Libyan subsidiary on December 7. The authors weighed the risk of Libyan retaliation against American interests against the value of a united consumer front against OPEC.
tripoli_details: The Libyan decree did not cover BP's 50 percent American partner, Bunker Hunt.
Bunker Hunt refused a Libyan request that it market the ex-BP share of the oil as well as its own.
The memo said the Libyan action followed frustration over unsettled claims against Britain, including former base rights, a cancelled air defense contract and non-delivery of Chieftain tanks.
The U.S. agreed to instruct embassies in OECD capitals to support the British demarches quietly.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d84.summary: In this January 7, 1972 letter Assistant Secretary Newsom told Ambassador Palmer in Tripoli that the Secretary of State would not change the policy of withholding decisions on military supplies to Libya. Newsom said the absence of a decision had not provoked any marked Libyan reaction, while a positive decision would raise public relations and Congressional problems.
tripoli_details: Newsom said he and Alex Johnson had been to the Secretary at least four times on the matter.
The letter discussed Lockheed's push to sell eight additional C-130s to Libya and the refusal to license air drop equipment.
United Aircraft's interest in selling helicopters to Libya was also covered.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d27.summary: In this September 24, 1973 cable the Embassy in Tripoli questioned whether the U.S. should keep the post open in the face of growing Libyan government hostility. The embassy said it had lost two key officers, restrictions had tightened, and asked the Department to set a timetable or commit to strengthening the mission.
tripoli_details: The embassy said Libya had made Arabic-in-passports a political issue and that the U.S. had not acquiesced.
The cable said the embassy's functions on property, nationalized American interests and protection of Americans were largely ineffective and mostly symbolic.
It said American oil interests in Libya had days that were numbered whether or not the post stayed.
It described the embassy as the victim of 'salami tactics' by the Libyan government.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d59.summary: In this June 2, 1970 letter Under Secretary Johnson asked Deputy Secretary of Defense Packard to review instructions on ending the economic assistance agreement with Libya. State argued that the U.S. owed Libya payments tied to its use of Wheelus and urged a conciliatory line to avoid harming relations.
tripoli_details: The agreement provided for $1,000,000 per year for the calendar years 1965 through 1971.
State's lawyers believed the U.S. owed $1,000,000 for 1968 and $906,840 for 1969, up to the November 19, 1969 end of effective use of Wheelus.
The draft telegram would let Ambassador Palmer acknowledge that the U.S. owed $1,906,840.
The memo said $7,000,000 was due the U.S. under the 1967 F-5 contract and a June 30, 1971 deadline applied to Wheelus-related claims.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d86.summary: This February 8, 1972 memo from Executive Secretary Eliot to Kissinger reports that the U.S. and Libya terminated nine bilateral agreements by an exchange of notes in Tripoli on February 5, including the 1955 military base agreement. The U.S. also agreed, at Libya's request, to withdraw its Military Liaison Staff from the Embassy in Tripoli by March 15.
tripoli_details: The exchange of notes in Tripoli on February 5, 1972 included an agreed mutual washout of financial claims.
Most of the agreements related to Wheelus Air Base, which had been evacuated in June 1970.
The Military Liaison Staff had helped the Libyan armed forces buy military supplies such as spare parts.
Eliot noted Libya had also recently asked for withdrawal of British military and naval missions.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d95.summary: In this December 7, 1972 cable the Embassy in Tripoli warned that a report of Foreign Minister Kikhya's remarks suggested the Libyan government might soon discriminate openly against American interests because of U.S. support for Israel. The embassy estimated this would likely begin in the first half of 1973 and urged the Department to settle the long-pending F-5 question.
tripoli_details: The embassy said possible targets included U.S. oil interests, commercial interests and the diplomatic presence, with a special tax on American oil companies or a partial boycott of American goods as possible measures.
It noted the U.S. Embassy staff was still larger than the Libyan Embassy in Washington by notified 'white list' personnel.
The embassy recommended delivering 8 F-5Bs, or else deciding not to deliver and telling Libya why.
It said Kikhya believed Libya had already paid $22 million for the F-5s.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d10.summary: In this April 5, 1973 cable the State Department told the Embassy in Tripoli to give the Libyan Foreign Ministry a note clarifying the U.S. view on 'restricted area' versus 'danger area' in international law. The note was to cite a March 21 incident in which a U.S. C-130 was fired on by Libyan Mirages.
tripoli_details: The Department said its investigation showed the C-130 was fired upon at 34 05 N, 14 20 E, 82 nautical miles from the Libyan coast.
The note was to avoid referring to the Libyan Ministry note of March 28, which the U.S. had rejected.
A footnote says the Embassy delivered the note on the morning of April 10.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d1.summary: This January 12, 1977 cable from the Embassy in Tunis reports Tunisian defense officials telling Admiral Bagley that an intelligence report said Qadhafi had outlined plans to 'unite' Libya with Tunisia by force. Tunisian Defense Minister Farhat said he took the report seriously.
tripoli_details: The report said Qadhafi held a secret meeting around January 1, 1977 and claimed to have obtained Soviet assurances of a hands-off policy during his Moscow visit.
Farhat believed Qadhafi was recruiting Egyptian, Iraqi and Palestinian mercenaries to make up for a lack of trained Libyans.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d142.summary: This November 14, 1980 memo from Secretary of State Muskie to President Carter reports that Libyan People's Bureau head Ali El-Houderi said Libya wanted improved relations. Libyan authorities had asked certain student leaders and a People's Committee member to leave the U.S.
tripoli_details: El-Houderi returned from Tripoli with guidance from Libyan authorities and said some students had already left.
Others would leave at the end of the fall semester, while some wished to stay and the Bureau claimed it could not compel them.
The People's Committee member had resigned and would leave after finishing his degree work in December.

frus-1981-88v24-d245.summary: This August 3, 1985 Secret cable relays President Reagan's letter to King Hassan, to be delivered by Deputy Secretary Whitehead. Reagan urged Hassan to avoid escalation in the Western Sahara and described Qadhafi's Libya as one of five states most directly involved in sponsoring international terrorism. He said Morocco's relationship with Qadhafi remained the major irritant between the two countries.
tripoli_details: Reagan wrote that he had publicly named Libya one of five states most directly involved in sponsoring international terrorism, after reviewing what the U.S. knew of activities spawned in Tripoli.
He said that Hassan had told General Walters the previous September he hoped to 'tame' Qadhafi, but the record showed no change in Qadhafi's policies.
Reagan wrote that Qadhafi sought to terrorize and assassinate Libyans at home and abroad who had a different vision for their country.
He said the U.S. believed the Libyan regime should be isolated politically and economically.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d64.summary: In this August 5, 1970 memo Secretary of State Rogers told President Nixon that Soviet medium tanks and armored personnel carriers had been delivered directly to Libya on July 20 to 22. He said this did not significantly change the regional arms balance, but raised concerns for US-Libyan relations, so Ambassador Palmer was being recalled for consultations.
tripoli_details: The Soviet equipment arrived directly from the USSR after Britain refused to supply the Chieftain tanks contracted for by the old regime.
The memo noted the U.S. had not said it would deliver the eight F-5s for which Libya held a valid contract, and Britain had suspended action on 188 Chieftain tanks.
Rogers said the way was open for the USSR to become a significant supplier and possibly establish a training mission in Libya.
He named the oil industry and the diplomatic presence as the two significant U.S. interests to preserve.

frus-1969-76ve05p2-d92.summary: In this September 1, 1972 memo NSC staffer Hoskinson advised Kissinger on whether to release eight F-5 aircraft to Libya. He reported that Secretary Rogers had just concluded that changing arms policy would not buy security for American oil companies, and recommended sticking with the current policy. Kissinger approved.
tripoli_details: Rogers judged the Libyans were probably bent on nationalizing the entire oil industry whenever it suited them.
Spares for previously supplied equipment would continue to be sold, and U.S. approval of the Italian sale of U.S.-origin armored personnel carriers and artillery would remain.
Hoskinson noted Qadhafi supported the fedayeen, subsidized Egypt and had made contributions to radical groups in the U.S. such as the Black Panthers.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d19.summary: This June 5, 1973 National Security Study Memorandum 185 from Kissinger ordered a study of U.S. policy toward Libya, to be done by State, Defense and the CIA and submitted by June 30, 1973. It covered Libyan terrorism, the Arab-Israeli dispute, subversion, international airspace and the petroleum industry.
tripoli_details: The study was to assess prospects for changed Libyan policies under Qadhafi or other leaders, including the effect of the possible Egyptian-Libyan merger.
It was to examine U.S. options on diplomatic relations, oil company operations, military supply and Libyan support for terrorism.

frus-1969-76ve09p1-d24.summary: In this August 30, 1973 cable the Chargé in Tripoli reported a dispute with the Libyan Foreign Ministry over passports. Libya said it would print its passports in English as well as Arabic, implying the U.S. might reciprocate with Arabic, but the Chargé rejected any such exchange and the embassy recommended standing firm.
tripoli_details: The U.S. position rested on the aide-memoire of November 15, 1972, and the principle of equal treatment.
The Libyan official Attiga said the Ministry had received instructions from the RCC on passports within the previous two days, and denied he was proposing a deal.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d20.summary: In this July 19, 1977 memo to President Carter, Secretary Vance reported a series of sharp Libyan attacks on several Egyptian border outposts over the previous 24 hours. State believed Qadhafi ordered them as a show of force, and that Egypt had responded with tactical air strikes.
tripoli_details: Vance wrote that Sadat was increasingly persuaded a military incursion into eastern Libya, or a raid on Tobruk, was the option with a chance of success.
He judged a major Egyptian-initiated escalation could not be ruled out within one to four weeks.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d199.summary: This March 24, 1979 cable reports Under Secretary Newsom's March 20 meeting with Tunisian Ambassador Hedda, which covered U.S. aid to Tunisia and a possible sale of Boeing 747s to Libya. Newsom said the 747 sale was under study and normalizing relations would be difficult as long as Libya supported international terrorism.
tripoli_details: Newsom said the U.S. had sold Libya 727s with the understanding they would not be used for military purposes, and that proof they were used in Uganda would affect the 747 decision.
He said Libya had made several approaches to improve relations.
Hedda said Tunisia saw little if any change in Libyan policy.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d121.summary: In this January 17, 1980 memo Brzezinski asked President Carter to approve a message to Qadhafi. He reported that Qadhafi's remark about Americans taking over the U.S. Embassy and turning it into a 'People's Bureau' was judged to be jocular, and proposed the chargé deliver the message and seek a direct meeting.
tripoli_details: A Congressional delegation was visiting Tripoli the next day, and Bill Eagleton might use the opportunity to request a one-on-one meeting with Qadhafi.
Qadhafi had suggested Americans take over the U.S. Embassy in Libya, as the Libyans had done in Washington.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d122.summary: This January 17, 1980 cable from Secretary Vance gave Chargé Eagleton in Tripoli talking points for a proposed meeting with Qadhafi. They asked for a designated Libyan security unit for the Embassy, ongoing liaison with Qadhafi's staff, and settlement of an embassy property claim.
tripoli_details: The U.S. asked for 24-hour communications access to a designated security unit, as the Libyan People's Bureau had in Washington.
It said an outstanding embassy property claim could be settled with property for a new Embassy building in Tripoli.
It raised the arrest of Embassy national employee Bashir Dultz.
Liaison was not to be only with Shahati or Turayki.

frus-1977-80v17p3-d51.summary: In this June 18, 1980 memo Gary Sick reported on an interagency meeting about the Egypt-Libya border after heated rhetoric. Participants judged that Egypt could take eastern Libya within a week but would not attack without escalating provocations.
tripoli_details: Sick wrote that Egypt outnumbered the Libyans three to one and had a two-division equivalent force in the Western Military District.
Impediments to an Egyptian attack included long supply lines and Libya's possible use of expatriate pilots.
No tangible acts by either side had backed up the heated exchange of words.
